papers.conclusion: The usage-based probing method allows tracking how grammatical number is encoded and transferred in BERT, showing that interventions impact behavior and extractability, revealing orthogonal encodings for nouns and verbs, and indirect transfer through intermediate tokens.
papers.key_findings:
BERT relies on a linear functional encoding of grammatical number to solve the number agreement task.
BERT uses separate encodings of grammatical number for nouns and verbs.
Number information is transferred from noun to verb between layers 3 and 8.
The transfer occurs indirectly through intermediate tokens, not directly via attention.
The encoding found by diagnostic probes is actually used by the model (functional).
papers.limitation:
The dataset may not be fully representative of the number agreement task.
Amnesic probing may remove more information than necessary.
papers.abstract: A central quest of probing is to uncover how pre-trained models encode a linguistic property within their representations. An encoding, however, might be spurious-i.e., the model might not rely on it when making predictions. In this paper, we try to find an encoding that the model actually uses, introducing a usage-based probing setup. We first choose a behavioral task which cannot be solved without using the linguistic property. Then, we attempt to remove the property by intervening on the model's representations. We contend that, if an encoding is used by the model, its removal should harm the performance on the chosen behavioral task. As a case study, we focus on how BERT encodes grammatical number, and on how it uses this encoding to solve the number agreement task. Experimentally, we find that BERT relies on a linear encoding of grammatical number to produce the correct behavioral output. We also find that BERT uses a separate encoding of grammatical number for nouns and verbs. Finally, we identify in which layers information about grammatical number is transferred from a noun to its head verb.

papers.title: Evaluating Layers of Representation in Neural Machine Translation on Part-of-Speech and Semantic Tagging Tasks
papers.research_question: What kind of linguistic information do neural machine translation models learn at different layers, specifically comparing part-of-speech and semantic tagging?
papers.core_contribution: Higher layers in NMT encoders are better at learning semantics while lower layers are better for part-of-speech tagging, and the effect of target language on source-side representations diminishes with larger training data.
papers.conclusion: Understanding how semantic properties are learned in NMT is a key step for creating better MT systems.
papers.key_findings:
Lower layer representations are usually better for POS tagging, while higher layer representations are better at capturing semantic information.
There is little effect of the target language on source-side representations, especially with higher quality NMT models trained on larger data.
English autoencoders produce poor representations for POS and SEM tagging compared to translation models, indicating that learning to translate is important for obtaining useful representations.
Bidirectional encoders and residual connections improve both translation and tagging performance.
The improvement from higher layers for semantic tagging is observed across different architectural variants and depths.
future_direction: Extend this work to other syntactic and semantic tasks that require building relations such as dependency relations or predicate-argument structure.
papers.abstract: While neural machine translation (NMT) models provide improved translation quality in an elegant, end-to-end framework, it is less clear what they learn about language. Recent work has started evaluating the quality of vector representations learned by NMT models on morphological and syntactic tasks. In this paper, we investigate the representations learned at different layers of NMT encoders. We train NMT systems on parallel data and use the trained models to extract features for training a classifier on two tasks: part-of-speech and semantic tagging. We then measure the performance of the classifier as a proxy to the quality of the original NMT model for the given task. Our quantitative analysis yields interesting insights regarding representation learning in NMT models. For instance, we find that higher layers are better at learning semantics while lower layers tend to be better for part-of-speech tagging. We also observe little effect of the target language on source-side representations, especially with higher quality NMT models.

papers.title: Accurate Word Alignment Induction from Neural Machine Translation
papers.research_question: Do attention weights in Transformer models capture accurate word alignments, and how can word alignments be better induced from neural machine translation models?
papers.core_contribution: This paper shows that Transformer attention weights can capture accurate word alignments if the correct decoding step and layer are chosen, and introduces two novel methods (SHIFT-ATT and SHIFT-AET) that induce alignments at the step when the target token is the decoder input, significantly improving alignment accuracy.
papers.conclusion: The proposed methods SHIFT-ATT and SHIFT-AET effectively induce word alignments from Transformer models, with SHIFT-AET achieving state-of-the-art performance without compromising translation quality.
papers.key_findings:
SHIFT-ATT, a pure interpretation method, reduces AER by 7.0-10.2 points over the NAIVE-ATT baseline and 5.5-7.9 points over FAST-ALIGN on three datasets.
SHIFT-AET, which adds and trains an alignment module supervised by SHIFT-ATT alignments, outperforms the statistical aligner GIZA++ by 1.4-4.8 AER points.
A proposed layer selection criterion, based on agreement between source-to-target and target-to-source model alignments, effectively identifies the best layer for alignment induction.
Both SHIFT-ATT and SHIFT-AET improve performance on the downstream task of dictionary-guided decoding compared to the NAIVE-ATT baseline.
Probing experiments show decoder hidden states at lower layers are more relevant to the input token than the output token, validating the shift in alignment step.
future_direction: Extend the study to more downstream tasks and systems.
papers.abstract: Despite its original goal to jointly learn to align and translate, prior researches suggest that Transformer captures poor word alignments through its attention mechanism. In this paper, we show that attention weights DO capture accurate word alignments and propose two novel word alignment induction methods SHIFT-ATT and SHIFT-AET. The main idea is to induce alignments at the step when the to-be-aligned target token is the decoder input rather than the decoder output as in previous work. SHIFT-ATT is an interpretation method that induces alignments from the attention weights of Transformer and does not require parameter update or architecture change. SHIFT-AET extracts alignments from an additional alignment module which is tightly integrated into Transformer and trained in isolation with supervision from symmetrized SHIFT-ATT alignments. Experiments on three publicly available datasets demonstrate that both methods perform better than their corresponding neural baselines and SHIFT-AET significantly outperforms GIZA++ by 1.4-4.8 AER points.

papers.title: The Geometry of Multilingual Language Model Representations
papers.research_question: How do multilingual language models maintain a shared multilingual representation space while still encoding language-sensitive information in each language?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that multilingual language models encode information along orthogonal language-sensitive and language-neutral axes, facilitating feature extraction for downstream tasks and cross-lingual transfer learning.
papers.conclusion: Multilingual language models encode features along orthogonal language-sensitive and language-neutral axes, enabling targeted extraction of features for downstream tasks and cross-lingual transfer learning.
papers.key_findings:
Languages occupy similar linear subspaces after mean-centering, as shown by causal effects on language modeling performance and direct subspace comparisons.
Subspace means differ along language-sensitive axes that encode information such as token vocabularies, and shifting representations by language means is sufficient to induce token predictions in different languages.
Stable language-neutral axes encode information such as token positions and part-of-speech, and these axes are orthogonal to language-sensitive axes.
The identified axes (both language-sensitive and language-neutral) are relatively stable across middle layers of the model.
Token position information is encoded along nonlinear structures like spirals, toruses, and curves in the representation space.
future_direction: Investigate how nonlinear structures (e.g., spirals, toruses) arise from and interact with the dot product self-attention mechanism in Transformer models.
Conduct a more detailed analysis of how specific representational structures are retained across layers.

Assess how multilingual language models encode more complex linguistic features geometrically, and the extent to which representation spaces can be fully decomposed into orthogonal subspaces encoding different features.
papers.abstract: We assess how multilingual language models maintain a shared multilingual representation space while still encoding language-sensitive information in each language. Using XLM-R as a case study, we show that languages occupy similar linear subspaces after mean-centering, evaluated based on causal effects on language modeling performance and direct comparisons between subspaces for 88 languages. The subspace means differ along language-sensitive axes that are relatively stable throughout middle layers, and these axes encode information such as token vocabularies. Shifting representations by language means is sufficient to induce token predictions in different languages. However, we also identify stable language-neutral axes that encode information such as token positions and part-of-speech. We visualize representations projected onto language-sensitive and language-neutral axes, identifying language family and part-of-speech clusters, along with spirals, toruses, and curves representing token position information. These results demonstrate that multilingual language models encode information along orthogonal language-sensitive and language-neutral axes, allowing the models to extract a variety of features for downstream tasks and cross-lingual transfer learning.

papers.title: Wide Attention Is The Way Forward For Transformers?
papers.research_question: What is the best model aspect ratio (balance between number of layers and attention heads per layer) for Transformers? Can wider, shallower Transformers match or outperform deeper ones in NLP tasks?
papers.core_contribution: Wider and shallower Transformer models, with a single layer and many parallel attention heads, can typically equal or sometimes outperform deeper models on NLP tasks when trained from scratch, while also being smaller, faster, and more interpretable.
papers.conclusion: Wider and shallower Transformers are a viable and desirable alternative to deeper models for small models on NLP tasks, offering comparable or better accuracy, smaller size, faster inference, and improved interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
On average across 4 NLP tasks and 10 attention types, single-layer wide models performed 0.3% better than their deeper counterparts.
Wider models are on average 71% the size of the deepest models, require a smaller memory footprint, and have faster inference latency (3.1x faster on CPU, 1.9x faster on GPU).
Single-layer wide models are more interpretable as attention weights from all heads can be inspected in one layer to understand classification decisions.
The performance benefit of going wider is task-dependent; the Listops task saw a 1.5% average accuracy increase, while other tasks had smaller changes.
For vision tasks (tested on CIFAR-10 with PVT-V2-B1), deeper Transformers remained superior, likely because pooling layers before attention capture crucial spatial information.
papers.limitation:
The study is limited to small models and tasks without pre-training; it remains to be seen if the results hold for much larger models on much larger datasets (e.g., masked language modeling).
For vision Transformers, the advantage of wider models is constrained because most vision Transformers use pooling or convolution layers before attention, which capture spatial information better in deeper architectures.
future_direction: Investigate whether the results hold for much larger models on much larger datasets, for example masked language modelling.
Explore wider and shallower models as an important area of research for domains beyond NLP.
papers.abstract: The Transformer is an extremely powerful and prominent deep learning architecture. In this work, we challenge the commonly held belief in deep learning that going deeper is better, and show an alternative design approach that is building wider attention Transformers. We demonstrate that wide single layer Transformer models can compete with or outperform deeper ones in a variety of Natural Language Processing (NLP) tasks when both are trained from scratch. The impact of changing the model aspect ratio on Transformers is then studied systematically. This ratio balances the number of layers and the number of attention heads per layer while keeping the total number of attention heads and all other hyperparameters constant. On average, across 4 NLP tasks and 10 attention types, single layer wide models perform 0.3% better than their deep counterparts. We show an in-depth evaluation and demonstrate how wide models require a far smaller memory footprint and can run faster on commodity hardware, in addition, these wider models are also more interpretable. For example, a single layer Transformer on the IMDb byte level text classification has 3.1x faster inference latency on a CPU than its equally accurate deeper counterpart, and is half the size. We therefore put forward wider and shallower models as a viable and desirable alternative for small models on NLP tasks, and as an important area of research for domains beyond this.

papers.title: Decoding Probing: Revealing Internal Linguistic Structures in Neural Language Models using Minimal Pairs
papers.research_question: How do neural language models capture linguistic information internally, specifically using minimal pairs to probe grammaticality across layers?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a novel 'decoding probing' method inspired by cognitive neuroscience to reveal internal linguistic structures in neural language models using minimal pairs, demonstrating that self-supervised models capture abstract linguistic features in intermediate layers with distinct patterns for syntax, morphology, and semantics.
papers.conclusion: Decoding probing bridges cognitive neuroscience and NLP, providing insights into hierarchical linguistic feature capture in LMs, with semantics-syntax interface and morphology being more challenging than syntax.
papers.key_findings:
Self-supervised language models capture abstract linguistic structures in intermediate layers that GloVe and RNN language models cannot learn.
Information about syntactic grammaticality is robustly captured through the first third layers of GPT-2 and distributed in later layers; more layers are required for complex sentences.
Morphological and semantics/syntax interface-related features are harder to capture than syntax.
For Transformer-based models, both embeddings and attentions capture grammatical features but show distinct patterns, with attention heads exhibiting similar tendencies but varied contributions.
papers.limitation: Focuses mainly on structure grammaticality with limited attention to conceptual capabilities.
future_direction: Apply decoding probe methods to reveal LM's ability to master concepts using the COMPS minimal pair dataset.
papers.abstract: Inspired by cognitive neuroscience studies, we introduce a novel `decoding probing' method that uses minimal pairs benchmark (BLiMP) to probe internal linguistic characteristics in neural language models layer by layer. By treating the language model as the `brain' and its representations as `neural activations', we decode grammaticality labels of minimal pairs from the intermediate layers' representations. This approach reveals: 1) Self-supervised language models capture abstract linguistic structures in intermediate layers that GloVe and RNN language models cannot learn. 2) Information about syntactic grammaticality is robustly captured through the first third layers of GPT-2 and also distributed in later layers. As sentence complexity increases, more layers are required for learning grammatical capabilities. 3) Morphological and semantics/syntax interface-related features are harder to capture than syntax. 4) For Transformer-based models, both embeddings and attentions capture grammatical features but show distinct patterns. Different attention heads exhibit similar tendencies toward various linguistic phenomena, but with varied contributions.

papers.title: Latent Positional Information is in the Self-Attention Variance of Transformer Language Models Without Positional Embeddings
papers.research_question: How is positional information encoded in transformer language models without positional embeddings?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that transformer language models without positional embeddings inherently encode positional information through the shrinkage of self-attention variance, both theoretically and empirically.
papers.conclusion: The analysis shows that positional information is encoded in self-attention variance, justifying the removal of positional embeddings for more efficient pretraining of transformer language models.
papers.key_findings:
Randomly initialized transformer language models without positional embeddings encode positional information in the variance of self-attention outputs, with variance decreasing as position increases.
This variance shrinkage effect persists after pre-training, especially in lower layers of the model.
BERT models fail to encode positional information without embeddings due to bidirectional attention masking.
Theoretical analysis shows that the variance of self-attention output is inversely proportional to token position.
Probing experiments confirm that positional information can be extracted from the model's internal representations.
papers.limitation: Assumptions of a randomly initialized and frozen TLM and randomly sampled input tokens do not hold for human languages and pre-trained models.
future_direction: Analyze the training dynamics of TLM to understand parameter distribution after pre-training.
Use Zipf's law or n-gram models to quantify input token duplication in human languages for better variance estimation.
papers.abstract: The use of positional embeddings in transformer language models is widely accepted. However, recent research has called into question the necessity of such embeddings. We further extend this inquiry by demonstrating that a randomly initialized and frozen transformer language model, devoid of positional embeddings, inherently encodes strong positional information through the shrinkage of self-attention variance. To quantify this variance, we derive the underlying distribution of each step within a transformer layer. Through empirical validation using a fully pretrained model, we show that the variance shrinkage effect still persists after extensive gradient updates. Our findings serve to justify the decision to discard positional embeddings and thus facilitate more efficient pretraining of transformer language models.

papers.title: BERTology Meets Biology: Interpreting Attention in Protein Language Models
papers.research_question: What does attention in protein Transformer language models capture about protein structure and function?
papers.core_contribution: Demonstrates that attention in protein language models captures high-level structural and functional properties of proteins, and that attention focuses on progressively more complex properties with increasing layer depth.
papers.conclusion: Attention in protein Transformer models recovers structural and functional properties of proteins, and interpretability methods can aid scientific discovery.
papers.key_findings:
Attention in deep layers aligns with contact maps, connecting amino acids that are spatially close in 3D structure but far in sequence.
Attention targets binding sites and post-translational modifications, key functional components.
Attention heads specialize in particular amino acids and their patterns are consistent with substitution matrices.
Deeper layers focus more on high-level properties (binding sites, contacts) while secondary structure is targeted more evenly across layers.
Knowledge in embeddings accumulates gradually over layers, while attention acquires knowledge primarily in final layers.
papers.limitation: The analyses are associative and do not establish causal links between attention and model behavior.
future_direction: Using attention and learned representations as tools for scientific discovery.
Developing contextual visualizations of learned representations for domain experts in scientific domains.
papers.abstract: Abstract Transformer architectures have proven to learn useful representations for protein classification and generation tasks. However, these representations present challenges in interpretability. Through the lens of attention, we analyze the inner workings of the Transformer and explore how the model discerns structural and functional properties of proteins. We show that attention (1) captures the folding structure of proteins, connecting amino acids that are far apart in the underlying sequence, but spatially close in the three-dimensional structure, (2) targets binding sites, a key functional component of proteins, and (3) focuses on progressively more complex biophysical properties with increasing layer depth. We also present a three-dimensional visualization of the interaction between attention and protein structure. Our findings align with known biological processes and provide a tool to aid discovery in protein engineering and synthetic biology. The code for visualization and analysis is available at https://github.com/salesforce/provis .

papers.title: Language Models Represent Space and Time
papers.research_question: Do large language models learn coherent linear representations of space and time, i.e., do they form a world model?
papers.core_contribution: Large language models learn linear representations of space and time that are robust to prompting and unified across entity types, and individual 'space' and 'time' neurons exist that encode these coordinates.
papers.conclusion: Modern LLMs learn rich spatiotemporal representations of the real world and possess basic ingredients of a world model.
papers.key_findings:
Linear probes can recover spatial and temporal coordinates from internal activations, with performance increasing with model size and plateauing in middle layers.
Spatial and temporal features are linearly represented, as nonlinear probes do not improve performance.
Representations are robust to variations in prompting, though random tokens or capitalization degrade performance.
Probes generalize across entity types and to held-out geographic or temporal blocks, indicating unified representations.
Individual neurons exist that are highly predictive of space and time, and causal interventions confirm their importance.
papers.limitation:
Data comes only from English Wikipedia, skewing towards the Anglosphere, and entity type distribution is not uniform.
The true extent and structure of spatial and temporal representations remain unclear.
future_direction: Extracting representations in the model’s coordinate system rather than human coordinates, e.g., with sparse autoencoders.
Studying how these spatiotemporal representations are learned, recalled, and used internally across training checkpoints.
Investigating potential parallels with biological place and grid cells in the brain.
papers.abstract: The capabilities of large language models (LLMs) have sparked debate over whether such systems just learn an enormous collection of superficial statistics or a set of more coherent and grounded representations that reflect the real world. We find evidence for the latter by analyzing the learned representations of three spatial datasets (world, US, NYC places) and three temporal datasets (historical figures, artworks, news headlines) in the Llama-2 family of models. We discover that LLMs learn linear representations of space and time across multiple scales. These representations are robust to prompting variations and unified across different entity types (e.g. cities and landmarks). In addition, we identify individual "space neurons" and "time neurons" that reliably encode spatial and temporal coordinates. While further investigation is needed, our results suggest modern LLMs learn rich spatiotemporal representations of the real world and possess basic ingredients of a world model.

papers.title: The Same But Different: Structural Similarities and Differences in Multilingual Language Modeling
papers.research_question: When two languages employ the same morphosyntactic processes, do LLMs handle them using shared internal circuitry? When two languages require different morphosyntactic processes, do LLMs handle them using different internal circuitry?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that LLMs use shared internal circuitry for similar syntactic processes across languages, even in independently trained monolingual models, and employ language-specific components (e.g., feed-forward networks) for language-specific morphological processes.
papers.conclusion: The paper finds that cross-lingual structural similarity is represented within LLMs using shared circuits that invoke the same algorithm independent of language, and that language-specific processing is localized to play a causal role only in languages that require it.
papers.key_findings:
Multilingual models use a single circuit to handle the same syntactic process independently of the language in which it occurs.
Monolingual models trained independently on English and Chinese each adopt nearly the same circuit for the IOI task, suggesting consistency in how LLMs learn to handle this aspect of language modeling.
For tasks requiring language-specific morphological processes (e.g., past tense marking in English), multilingual models invoke a largely overlapping circuit but employ language-specific components as needed, such as feed-forward networks in English only for morphological marking.
The circuits identified for the IOI task align with prior work, indicating that the same mechanism is shared between English and Chinese within a multilingual model.
Heads specifically responsible for past tense disambiguation are activated in English but not in Chinese, and they suppress present-tense verbs in English.
papers.limitation: Results are limited to specific tasks and datasets, requiring future work for replication and generalization.
future_direction: Replicate and generalize findings to more tasks and datasets.
Explore cross-disciplinary collaborations to gain fresh perspectives on linguistic universality using LLMs.
Investigate whether circuit overlap can be exploited for improving cross-lingual transfer and safety.
papers.abstract: We employ new tools from mechanistic interpretability in order to ask whether the internal structure of large language models (LLMs) shows correspondence to the linguistic structures which underlie the languages on which they are trained. In particular, we ask (1) when two languages employ the same morphosyntactic processes, do LLMs handle them using shared internal circuitry? and (2) when two languages require different morphosyntactic processes, do LLMs handle them using different internal circuitry? Using English and Chinese multilingual and monolingual models, we analyze the internal circuitry involved in two tasks. We find evidence that models employ the same circuit to handle the same syntactic process independently of the language in which it occurs, and that this is the case even for monolingual models trained completely independently. Moreover, we show that multilingual models employ language-specific components (attention heads and feed-forward networks) when needed to handle linguistic processes (e.g., morphological marking) that only exist in some languages. Together, our results provide new insights into how LLMs trade off between exploiting common structures and preserving linguistic differences when tasked with modeling multiple languages simultaneously.

papers.title: Language Ranker: A Metric for Quantifying LLM Performance Across High and Low-Resource Languages
papers.research_question: How can we quantify the performance of LLMs across different languages, especially low-resource ones, using internal representations?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes Language Ranker, an intrinsic metric that benchmarks and ranks languages based on LLM performance by comparing internal representations to an English baseline, revealing performance disparities between high and low-resource languages.
papers.conclusion: Language Ranker effectively quantifies LLM performance across languages, showing that high-resource languages perform better and are more evenly distributed in embedding space, and that performance correlates with training data proportion.
papers.key_findings:
High-resource languages exhibit higher similarity scores with English, indicating better performance, while low-resource languages show lower similarity scores.
There is a strong correlation between LLM performance in a language and the proportion of that language in the pre-training corpus.
High-resource languages are more evenly distributed in the embedding space, while low-resource languages cluster narrowly.
The proposed cosine similarity metric correlates with performance on reasoning tasks (ARC and MMLU).
Different LLMs show consistent language performance rankings, as measured by rank correlation.
future_direction: Design more comprehensive benchmarks to measure LLM capabilities in different languages.
Develop nuanced evaluation metrics that capture syntactic and semantic understanding across language families.
Apply Language Ranker insights to guide the development of more balanced multilingual training datasets and inform architectural improvements.
papers.abstract: The development of Large Language Models (LLMs) relies on extensive text corpora, which are often unevenly distributed across languages. This imbalance results in LLMs performing significantly better on high-resource languages like English, German, and French, while their capabilities in low-resource languages remain inadequate. Currently, there is a lack of quantitative methods to evaluate the performance of LLMs in these low-resource languages. To address this gap, we propose the Language Ranker, an intrinsic metric designed to benchmark and rank languages based on LLM performance using internal representations. By comparing the LLM's internal representation of various languages against a baseline derived from English, we can assess the model's multilingual capabilities in a robust and language-agnostic manner. Our analysis reveals that high-resource languages exhibit higher similarity scores with English, demonstrating superior performance, while low-resource languages show lower similarity scores, underscoring the effectiveness of our metric in assessing language-specific capabilities. Besides, the experiments show that there is a strong correlation between the LLM’s performance in different languages and the proportion of those languages in its pre-training corpus. These insights underscore the efficacy of the Language Ranker as a tool for evaluating LLM performance across different languages, particularly those with limited resources.

papers.title: Quantifying Language Models' Sensitivity to Spurious Features in Prompt Design or: How I learned to start worrying about prompt formatting
papers.research_question: How sensitive are large language models to subtle, meaning-preserving changes in prompt formatting?
papers.core_contribution: This paper demonstrates that LLMs are extremely sensitive to semantically equivalent prompt formatting choices, and introduces FORMAT SPREAD, a method to efficiently estimate the performance spread across plausible formats without accessing model weights.
papers.conclusion: The paper argues that research evaluating LLMs with prompting should report performance across a range of plausible prompt formats rather than a single format, and that FORMAT SPREAD facilitates this systematic analysis.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs show extreme sensitivity to prompt formatting, with performance differences of up to 76 accuracy points between equivalent formats.
Sensitivity persists even when increasing model size, the number of few-shot examples, or with instruction tuning.
Format performance only weakly correlates between models, questioning the validity of comparing models with a single, fixed prompt format.
Small atomic changes in format (e.g., casing, separators) can lead to large, unpredictable accuracy changes.
Prompt formats are highly identifiable from the model's internal representations (prompt embeddings), and this identifiability correlates with performance spread.
papers.limitation: Some generated prompt formats may be unnatural (e.g., due to parsing choices or unusual separators), and the study is limited to tasks with reasonably short input instructions and field length.
papers.abstract: As large language models (LLMs) are adopted as a fundamental component of language technologies, it is crucial to accurately characterize their performance. Because choices in prompt design can strongly influence model behavior, this design process is critical in effectively using any modern pre-trained generative language model. In this work, we focus on LLM sensitivity to a quintessential class of meaning-preserving design choices: prompt formatting. We find that several widely used open-source LLMs are extremely sensitive to subtle changes in prompt formatting in few-shot settings, with performance differences of up to 76 accuracy points when evaluated using LLaMA-2-13B. Sensitivity remains even when increasing model size, the number of few-shot examples, or performing instruction tuning. Our analysis suggests that work evaluating LLMs with prompting-based methods would benefit from reporting a range of performance across plausible prompt formats, instead of the currently-standard practice of reporting performance on a single format. We also show that format performance only weakly correlates between models, which puts into question the methodological validity of comparing models with an arbitrarily chosen, fixed prompt format. To facilitate systematic analysis we propose FormatSpread, an algorithm that rapidly evaluates a sampled set of plausible prompt formats for a given task, and reports the interval of expected performance without accessing model weights. Furthermore, we present a suite of analyses that characterize the nature of this sensitivity, including exploring the influence of particular atomic perturbations and the internal representation of particular formats.

papers.title: Neuron Specialization: Leveraging intrinsic task modularity for multilingual machine translation
papers.research_question: How do neurons in multilingual translation models exhibit language-specific modularity, and can this be leveraged to reduce interference and improve translation performance?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that FFN neurons in multilingual models exhibit language-specific modularity, and introduces Neuron Specialization, a method that leverages this to reduce interference and improve translation performance.
papers.conclusion: The paper shows that intrinsic modularity in multilingual models can be leveraged to improve translation performance by reducing interference and enhancing transfer, with Neuron Specialization providing consistent gains.
papers.key_findings:
FFN neurons in multilingual translation models activate in a language-specific way, with overlaps indicating linguistic proximity.
The specialization of neurons evolves across layers, becoming more language-agnostic in the encoder and more specific in the decoder.
The proposed Neuron Specialization method, which updates task-specific neurons via sparse networks, consistently improves translation quality over baselines.
This method effectively reduces negative interference in high-resource languages and boosts knowledge transfer in low-resource languages.
Neuron Specialization is efficient, requiring minimal extra parameters and time compared to adapter-based methods.
papers.limitation:
The study is limited to multilingual machine translation and does not explore other multilingual NLP tasks.
Analysis is confined to feed-forward network components, excluding other Transformer elements like attention mechanisms.
Neuron identification relies on ReLU activation states; other activation functions like GELU are not considered.
future_direction: Extend the exploration to a broader range of Multilingual Natural Language Processing tasks beyond translation.
Investigate the modularity of other Transformer components such as attention mechanisms or layer normalization.
Explore neuron specialization for FFNs using activation functions other than ReLU, such as GELU.
papers.abstract: Training a unified multilingual model promotes knowledge transfer but inevitably introduces negative interference. Language-specific modeling methods show promise in reducing interference. However, they often rely on heuristics to distribute capacity and struggle to foster cross-lingual transfer via isolated modules. In this paper, we explore intrinsic task modularity within multilingual networks and leverage these observations to circumvent interference under multilingual translation. We show that neurons in the feed-forward layers tend to be activated in a language-specific manner. Meanwhile, these specialized neurons exhibit structural overlaps that reflect language proximity, which progress across layers. Based on these findings, we propose Neuron Specialization, an approach that identifies specialized neurons to modularize feed-forward layers and then continuously updates them through sparse networks. Extensive experiments show that our approach achieves consistent performance gains over strong baselines with additional analyses demonstrating reduced interference and increased knowledge transfer.

papers.title: The Generalization Ridge: Information Flow in Natural Language Generation
papers.research_question: In NLG, how does information evolve across layers during training, and how are different layers of the network functionally organized to support generalization versus memorization?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces InfoRidge, an information-theoretic framework, and uses it to reveal a 'generalization ridge' in intermediate layers where predictive information peaks, indicating a trade-off between generalization and memorization.
papers.conclusion: The findings reveal a consistent generalization ridge in intermediate layers, reflecting a fundamental trade-off between generalization and memorization as information flows deeper into the model.
papers.key_findings:
Predictive information peaks at intermediate layers (the 'generalization ridge') and then declines in final layers.
Incremental information gain is highest in intermediate layers.
Attention patterns show that intermediate layers attend to task-relevant (signal) tokens.
Residual scaling experiments show that under distribution shift, the model relies less on final layers and more on intermediate layers.
The generalization ridge phenomenon persists in multi-token generation scenarios.
papers.abstract: Transformer-based language models have achieved state-of-the-art performance in natural language generation (NLG), yet their internal mechanisms for synthesizing task-relevant information remain insufficiently understood. While prior studies suggest that intermediate layers often yield more generalizable representations than final layers, how this generalization ability emerges and propagates across layers during training remains unclear. To address this gap, we propose InfoRidge, an information-theoretic framework, to characterize how predictive information-the mutual information between hidden representations and target outputs-varies across depth during training. Our experiments across various models and datasets reveal a consistent non-monotonic trend: predictive information peaks in intermediate layers-forming a generalization ridge-before declining in final layers, reflecting a transition between generalization and memorization. To further investigate this phenomenon, we conduct a set of complementary analyses that leverage residual scaling, attention pattern, and controlled model capacity to characterize layer-wise functional specialization. We further validate our findings with multiple-token generation experiments, verifying that the observed ridge phenomenon persists across decoding steps. Together, these findings offer new insights into the internal mechanisms of transformers and underscore the critical role of intermediate layers in supporting generalization.

papers.title: Visualizing Attention in Transformer-Based Language Representation Models
papers.core_contribution: The paper presents an open-source visualization tool for multi-head self-attention in Transformer-based language models, extending prior work with three granularity levels (attention-head, model, and neuron views) and demonstrating its use on BERT and GPT-2.
papers.conclusion: The paper presents a tool for visualizing attention in Transformer-based language models, demonstrates its application on BERT and GPT-2, and outlines future work including empirical evaluation and interface integration.
papers.key_findings:
The tool can visualize attention patterns at three levels, revealing positional and lexical patterns in attention heads.
The attention-head view can be used to detect potential model bias, such as gender bias in coreference resolution in GPT-2.
The model view can identify recurring patterns, such as null attention to the first token, suggesting a potential design improvement.
The neuron view can link specific neurons in the query and key vectors to model behavior, such as a distance-decaying attention pattern.
The tool provides actionable insights for model interpretation and potential intervention, such as manipulating neurons to control attention behavior.
future_direction: Empirically evaluate how attention impacts model predictions across a range of tasks.
Integrate the three views (attention-head, model, neuron) into a unified interface.
Visualize the value vectors in addition to the queries and keys, and enable users to manipulate the model by modifying attention or editing individual neurons.
papers.abstract: We present an open-source tool for visualizing multi-head self-attention in Transformer-based language representation models. The tool extends earlier work by visualizing attention at three levels of granularity: the attention-head level, the model level, and the neuron level. We describe how each of these views can help to interpret the model, and we demonstrate the tool on the BERT model and the OpenAI GPT-2 model. We also present three use cases for analyzing GPT-2: detecting model bias, identifying recurring patterns, and linking neurons to model behavior.

papers.title: On the Interplay Between Fine-tuning and Sentence-level Probing for Linguistic Knowledge in Pre-trained Transformers
papers.research_question: How does fine-tuning affect the representations and linguistic knowledge in pre-trained transformer models, and to what extent can changes in probing accuracy be attributed to changes in linguistic knowledge?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that fine-tuning pre-trained transformer models affects sentence-level probing accuracy, but these changes are not straightforward and often not due to acquisition or loss of linguistic knowledge; instead, they can be attributed to changes in attention distribution or other factors, requiring careful interpretation.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that fine-tuning can lead to substantial changes in probing accuracy, but these changes require careful interpretation as they may not directly indicate changes in linguistic knowledge.
papers.key_findings:
Fine-tuning affects probing accuracy, with changes typically larger for higher layers.
Changes in probing accuracy vary across models, fine-tuning tasks, and probing tasks.
Improvements in probing accuracy with CLS-pooling can be attributed to changes in attention distribution rather than acquisition of new linguistic knowledge.
Fine-tuning can negatively affect probing accuracy, possibly due to changes in representations.
Only in few cases does fine-tuning improve probing accuracy beyond using a strong pooling method like mean-pooling.
papers.limitation: It remains unclear whether fine-tuning indeed removes the linguistic knowledge or whether it is simply no longer linearly separable.
future_direction: Further investigation into whether fine-tuning removes linguistic knowledge or just makes it not linearly separable.
papers.abstract: Fine-tuning pre-trained contextualized embedding models has become an integral part of the NLP pipeline. At the same time, probing has emerged as a way to investigate the linguistic knowledge captured by pre-trained models. Very little is, however, understood about how fine-tuning affects the representations of pre-trained models and thereby the linguistic knowledge they encode. This paper contributes towards closing this gap. We study three different pre-trained models: BERT, RoBERTa, and ALBERT, and investigate through sentence-level probing how finetuning affects their representations. We find that for some probing tasks fine-tuning leads to substantial changes in accuracy, possibly suggesting that fine-tuning introduces or even removes linguistic knowledge from a pre-trained model. These changes, however, vary greatly across different models, fine-tuning and probing tasks. Our analysis reveals that while finetuning indeed changes the representations of a pre-trained model and these changes are typically larger for higher layers, only in very few cases, fine-tuning has a positive effect on probing accuracy that is larger than just using the pre-trained model with a strong pooling method. Based on our findings, we argue that both positive and negative effects of finetuning on probing require a careful interpretation.

papers.title: The Hidden Space of Transformer Language Adapters
papers.research_question: How do transformer language adapters internally adapt predictions from a source language to a target language?
papers.core_contribution: Language adapters gradually evolve predictions in the source language, with the target language becoming pronounced only in the last layers, and they preserve the structure of the pre-trained model's representation space.
papers.conclusion: The study reveals that language adaptation via adapters is gradual and constrained by the pre-trained model's representation space, with implications for efficient adaptation.
papers.key_findings:
Adapted predictions are evolved in the source language distribution until the last few layers.
The adaptation process is distributed across layers with gradual updates.
Adapters can often be removed without decreasing performance, except for the last few layers.
Adapters operate on top of the model's representation space, preserving its structure, rather than in an isolated subspace.
papers.limitation:
Experiments are conducted on models trained from scratch using a relatively small corpus.
Reliance on projecting hidden representations to vocabulary space, which is an approximation.
Focus on only 8 specific target languages.
future_direction: Designing more efficient adaptation approaches based on language similarity.
Extending analysis to existing multilingual models like mGPT.
Investigating alternative adaptation methods less constrained by pre-trained structure.
papers.abstract: We analyze the operation of transformer language adapters, which are small modules trained on top of a frozen language model to adapt its predictions to new target languages. We show that adapted predictions mostly evolve in the source language the model was trained on, while the target language becomes pronounced only in the very last layers of the model. Moreover, the adaptation process is gradual and distributed across layers, where it is possible to skip small groups of adapters without decreasing adaptation performance. Last, we show that adapters operate on top of the model's frozen representation space while largely preserving its structure, rather than on an 'isolated' subspace. Our findings provide a deeper view into the adaptation process of language models to new languages, showcasing the constraints imposed on it by the underlying model and introduces practical implications to enhance its efficiency.

papers.title: When Less Language is More: Language-Reasoning Disentanglement Makes LLMs Better Multilingual Reasoners
papers.research_question: Can reasoning and language processing in LLMs be disentangled to improve multilingual reasoning performance?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that reasoning and language can be disentangled in LLMs by ablating language-specific components in hidden states, leading to improved multilingual reasoning performance across diverse models and languages.
papers.conclusion: The findings demonstrate that language and reasoning are separable in LLMs, and the proposed training-free intervention provides a lightweight and interpretable strategy for improving cross-lingual generalization.
papers.key_findings:
Language-reasoning disentanglement via activation ablation consistently improves multilingual reasoning performance across 10 open-weight LLMs and 11 typologically diverse languages.
There is a negative correlation between language-specific activation and reasoning accuracy; removing language-specific signals improves reasoning.
Middle layers are most effective for disentanglement, improving reasoning while preserving language fidelity, whereas upper-layer ablation degrades output fluency.
The training-free intervention achieves comparable or superior results to post-training methods like supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning.
Low-resource languages show a trade-off: reasoning improves with ablation, but language fidelity drops more sharply than in high-resource languages.
papers.limitation:
After ablation, models tend to default to English, which may reduce language fidelity, especially for low-resource languages.
The exact ratios of pretraining data for different languages are unknown, which limits a definitive explanation of the convergence phenomenon.
future_direction: Further investigation into the convergence of non-English representations to English after ablation.
Exploring adaptive ablation strategies to balance reasoning improvement and language fluency for low-resource languages.
Combining the training-free intervention with post-training methods for enhanced multilingual reasoning.
papers.abstract: Multilingual reasoning remains a significant challenge for large language models (LLMs), with performance disproportionately favoring high-resource languages. Drawing inspiration from cognitive neuroscience, which suggests that human reasoning functions largely independently of language processing, we hypothesize that LLMs similarly encode reasoning and language as separable components that can be disentangled to enhance multilingual reasoning. To evaluate this, we perform a causal intervention by ablating language-specific representations at inference time. Experiments on 10 open-weight LLMs spanning 11 typologically diverse languages show that this language-specific ablation consistently boosts multilingual reasoning performance. Layer-wise analyses further confirm that language and reasoning representations can be effectively disentangled throughout the model, yielding improved multilingual reasoning capabilities, while preserving top-layer language features remains essential for maintaining linguistic fidelity. Compared to post-training methods such as supervised fine-tuning or reinforcement learning, our training-free language-reasoning disentanglement achieves comparable or superior results with minimal computational overhead. These findings shed light on the internal mechanisms underlying multilingual reasoning in LLMs and suggest a lightweight and interpretable strategy for improving cross-lingual generalization.

papers.title: A Shared Geometry of Difficulty in Multilingual Language Models
papers.research_question: Whether problem-difficulty representations in multilingual LLMs are language-specific or shared across languages, and how they are encoded depth-dependently.
papers.core_contribution: LLMs encode problem difficulty in a depth-dependent manner: early layers form a language-agnostic representation that supports cross-lingual transfer, while deeper layers refine it into language-specific representations.
papers.conclusion: LLMs form a language-agnostic estimate of difficulty in early layers before specializing it to individual languages in deeper layers, indicating a shared geometry of difficulty across languages.
papers.key_findings:
Difficulty is linearly decodable from both shallow (early) and deep (later) transformer layers.
Probes trained on shallow representations generalize substantially better across languages than those trained on deep representations.
Probes trained on deep representations achieve higher accuracy within the same language but generalize poorly across languages.
There is a trade-off between cross-lingual generalization and language-specific accuracy, with optimal layers differing for same-language vs. cross-lingual evaluation.
This depth-dependent organization of difficulty representations is consistent across multiple LLM architectures and scales.
papers.limitation:
Analysis is confined to mathematical problem solving using the AMC subset of Easy2Hard, so it is unclear if findings extend to other domains.
Empirical evaluation is limited to a small set of instruction-tuned, decoder-only language models.
Conclusions are based exclusively on probing analyses without causal evidence for the role of difficulty signals in inference.
future_direction: Whether difficulty-based interventions learned in one language transfer to other languages.
papers.abstract: Predicting problem-difficulty in large language models (LLMs) refers to estimating how difficult a task is according to the model itself, typically by training linear probes on its internal representations. In this work, we study the multilingual geometry of problem-difficulty in LLMs by training linear probes using the AMC subset of the Easy2Hard benchmark, translated into 21 languages. We found that difficulty-related signals emerge at two distinct stages of the model internals, corresponding to shallow (early-layers) and deep (later-layers) internal representations, that exhibit functionally different behaviors. Probes trained on deep representations achieve high accuracy when evaluated on the same language but exhibit poor cross-lingual generalization. In contrast, probes trained on shallow representations generalize substantially better across languages, despite achieving lower within-language performance. Together, these results suggest that LLMs first form a language-agnostic representation of problem difficulty, which subsequently becomes language-specific. This closely aligns with existing findings in LLM interpretability showing that models tend to operate in an abstract conceptual space before producing language-specific outputs. We demonstrate that this two-stage representational process extends beyond semantic content to high-level meta-cognitive properties such as problem-difficulty estimation.

papers.title: Transformer Language Models without Positional Encodings Still Learn Positional Information
papers.research_question: Can transformer language models learn positional information without explicit positional encodings, and how do they do it?
papers.core_contribution: Transformer language models without explicit positional encodings (NoPos) can learn implicit positional information and achieve competitive performance, and this ability is due to the causal attention mask.
papers.conclusion: Transformer language models can learn positional information without explicit encodings, and this phenomenon is robust across settings but does not extend to masked language models, with the causal attention mechanism being the key factor.
papers.key_findings:
NoPos models achieve competitive perplexity compared to models with explicit positional encodings across different datasets, model sizes, and sequence lengths.
Probing experiments show that NoPos models learn an implicit notion of absolute positions in their hidden representations, similar to models with learned positional embeddings.
The success of NoPos models is unique to causal language models; masked language models fail to converge without positional encodings.
Shuffling the prefix tokens leads to a dramatic increase in loss, indicating that the model uses the learned positional information.
The causal attention mask is conjectured to allow the model to infer absolute positions by counting the number of attendable tokens.
papers.limitation:
Experiments are limited to models up to 1.3B parameters, and while the trend suggests the findings should hold for larger models, this is not tested.
NoPos models are always slightly worse than models with positional encodings, indicating that the inductive bias of positional encoding is important.
papers.abstract: Causal transformer language models (LMs), such as GPT-3, typically require some form of positional encoding, such as positional embeddings. However, we show that LMs without any explicit positional encoding are still competitive with standard models and that this phenomenon is robust across different datasets, model sizes, and sequence lengths.Probing experiments reveal that such models acquire an implicit notion of absolute positions throughout the network, effectively compensating for the missing information.We conjecture that causal attention enables the model to infer the number of predecessors that each token can attend to, thereby approximating its absolute position.Our findings indicate that causal LMs might derive positional awareness not only from the explicit positioning mechanism but also from the effects of the causal mask.

papers.title: A quantitative analysis of semantic information in deep representations of text and images
papers.research_question: How does semantic information converge across languages, modalities, and architectures in deep representations, and how can we quantify the directed predictability between representations?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that semantic information in deep representations is spread across many tokens and is strongest in central layers for autoregressive models and final layers for encoder models, with information asymmetries depending on language, model scale, and modality.
papers.conclusion: The results support the hypothesis of semantic convergence across languages, modalities, and architectures, while showing that directed predictability between representations varies strongly with layer-depth, model scale, and language.
papers.key_findings:
Semantic information is spread across many tokens in deep layers, not concentrated in the last token.
For autoregressive models (like DeepSeek-V3), semantic predictability is strongest in central layers, while for encoder models (like DinoV2) it is strongest in the final layers.
Information asymmetries exist: English representations are more predictive of translations than other languages, and larger models (DeepSeek-V3) are more predictive of smaller models (Llama3-8b) than the reverse.
Cross-modal predictability between independently trained large models (DeepSeek-V3 and DinoV2) can be stronger than that of jointly trained multimodal models (CLIP), suggesting model scale may outweigh explicit multimodal training.
The Information Imbalance metric is effective in quantifying directed predictability between representations, outperforming symmetric metrics like CKA and NO in high-dimensional settings.
papers.abstract: Deep neural networks are known to develop similar representations for semantically related data, even when they belong to different domains, such as an image and its description, or the same text in different languages. We present a method for quantitatively investigating this phenomenon by measuring the relative information content of the representations of semantically related data and probing how it is encoded into multiple tokens of large language models (LLMs) and vision transformers. Looking first at how LLMs process pairs of translated sentences, we identify inner ``semantic'' layers containing the most language-transferable information. We find moreover that, on these layers, a larger LLM (DeepSeek-V3) extracts significantly more general information than a smaller one (Llama3.1-8B). Semantic information of English text is spread across many tokens and it is characterized by long-distance correlations between tokens and by a causal left-to-right (i.e., past-future) asymmetry. We also identify layers encoding semantic information within visual transformers. We show that caption representations in the semantic layers of LLMs predict visual representations of the corresponding images. We observe significant and model-dependent information asymmetries between image and text representations.

papers.title: How Language Directions Align with Token Geometry in Multilingual LLMs
papers.research_question: Where and how is language information encoded within transformer layers? Does the pretraining language distribution structurally reshape the geometry of multilingual representations?
papers.core_contribution: Language information in multilingual LLMs is linearly separable from the first transformer block and remains stable across layers, and the alignment between language directions and vocabulary embeddings is shaped by pretraining data composition, indicating structural imprinting.
papers.conclusion: Language representation in LLMs is distinguished by latent representational structures formed during pretraining, established early and preserved across layers, highlighting the importance of balanced language composition for fairness and robustness.
papers.key_findings:
Language information becomes sharply separated in the first transformer block (+76.4±8.2%p from Layer 0→1) and remains almost fully linearly separable throughout model depth.
The alignment between language directions and vocabulary embeddings is strongly tied to the language composition of the training data, with Chinese-inclusive models showing 4.21× higher alignment for Chinese compared to English-centric models.
Chinese reaches maximal separability in deeper layers, whereas Spanish and German converge earlier, showing typological effects.
Linear probes achieve 99.8±0.1% accuracy on average, with only a 0.58±0.12%p gap relative to MLP probes, indicating linear separability.
Match@Peak remains low for Latin-script languages, suggesting language directions capture abstract features beyond token identity.
papers.limitation: The study is limited to five languages and may not generalize to all languages or scripts.
future_direction: expanding the analysis to additional languages and scripts
evaluating the influence of tokenizer design
conducting interventional studies
papers.abstract: Multilingual LLMs demonstrate strong performance across diverse languages, yet there has been limited systematic analysis of how language information is structured within their internal representation space and how it emerges across layers. We conduct a comprehensive probing study on six multilingual LLMs, covering all 268 transformer layers, using linear and nonlinear probes together with a new Token--Language Alignment analysis to quantify the layer-wise dynamics and geometric structure of language encoding. Our results show that language information becomes sharply separated in the first transformer block (+76.4$\pm$8.2 percentage points from Layer 0 to 1) and remains almost fully linearly separable throughout model depth. We further find that the alignment between language directions and vocabulary embeddings is strongly tied to the language composition of the training data. Notably, Chinese-inclusive models achieve a ZH Match@Peak of 16.43\%, whereas English-centric models achieve only 3.90\%, revealing a 4.21$\times$ structural imprinting effect. These findings indicate that multilingual LLMs distinguish languages not by surface script features but by latent representational structures shaped by the training corpus. Our analysis provides practical insights for data composition strategies and fairness in multilingual representation learning. All code and analysis scripts are publicly available at: https://github.com/thisiskorea/How-Language-Directions-Align-with-Token-Geometry-in-Multilingual-LLMs.

papers.title: Probing Word Translations in the Transformer and Trading Decoder for Encoder Layers
papers.research_question: How does word translation evolve across Transformer layers? Which role does each layer play in word translation?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that word translation progressively happens in encoder layers and even in input embeddings, and that some decoder layers contribute little. This motivates trading decoder layers for encoder layers, which can improve decoding speed and translation quality.
papers.conclusion: The analysis reveals the existence of target translations in encoder states and shows that trading decoder for encoder layers can lead to significant BLEU improvements while boosting decoding speed.
papers.key_findings:
Translation already happens progressively in encoder layers and even in the input embeddings.
Some lower decoder layers do not contribute significantly to word translation.
Increasing the number of encoder layers while decreasing decoder layers can boost decoding speed without loss in translation quality.
A configuration with 18 encoder and 4 decoder layers improves BLEU by +1.42 (En-De) with a speed-up of 1.4x.
The source context (cross-attention) is more important than decoding history (self-attention) in deep decoder layers.
papers.limitation: The probing approach uses attention matrices from the decoder to align source and target tokens, which might introduce dependencies.
papers.abstract: Due to its effectiveness and performance, the Transformer translation model has attracted wide attention, most recently in terms of probing-based approaches. Previous work focuses on using or probing source linguistic features in the encoder. To date, the way word translation evolves in Transformer layers has not yet been investigated. Naively, one might assume that encoder layers capture source information while decoder layers translate. In this work, we show that this is not quite the case: translation already happens progressively in encoder layers and even in the input embeddings. More surprisingly, we find that some of the lower decoder layers do not actually do that much decoding. We show all of this in terms of a probing approach where we project representations of the layer analyzed to the final trained and frozen classifier level of the Transformer decoder to measure word translation accuracy. Our findings motivate and explain a Transformer configuration change: if translation already happens in the encoder layers, perhaps we can increase the number of encoder layers, while decreasing the number of decoder layers, boosting decoding speed, without loss in translation quality? Our experiments show that this is indeed the case: we can increase speed by up to a factor 2.3 with small gains in translation quality, while an 18-4 deep encoder configuration boosts translation quality by +1.42 BLEU (En-De) at a speed-up of 1.4.

papers.title: Probing Context Localization of Polysemous Words in Pre-trained Language Model Sub-Layers
papers.research_question: How does the degree of contextualization for polysemous words vary across the fine-grained sub-layer representations (Self-Attention, Feed-Forward Activation, Output) of a pre-trained language model, and how is it influenced by word position and context length?
papers.core_contribution: The degree of contextualization in BERT sub-layers for polysemous words is not uniform and is significantly influenced by word position and context length, with shorter contexts leading to higher contextualization in upper layers, while longer contexts show different behavior across sub-layers.
papers.conclusion: The study provides a cautionary conclusion that the degree of contextualization in BERT sub-layers varies with word position and context window, and that linear probing has limitations in capturing word sense in longer contexts, suggesting these factors must be considered when interpreting model representations.
papers.key_findings:
For shorter context windows, the Output sub-layer shows lower contextualization (higher similarity) compared to Self-Attention and Feed-Forward Activation sub-layers, with higher contextualization observed in upper BERT layers.
For longer context windows, the Feed-Forward Activation sub-layer shows the highest dissimilarity (contextualization) in lower BERT layers compared to other sub-layers.
Linear sense probes perform well on the short-context CPWS dataset, indicating sense information is encoded in middle and upper BERT layers, but perform poorly on the longer-context sPWC and PWC datasets.
The similarity between sub-layer representations and static word embeddings (WESim) shows that Self-Attention sub-layer similarities remain consistent across layers, while Output sub-layer similarities shift from lower to upper layers as context window varies.
T-SNE visualization shows that different senses form separable clusters for the short-context CPWS dataset but not for the longer-context PWC dataset.
papers.limitation:
The experiments do not consider the syntactic structure (e.g., subject-verb agreement) of the sample sentences.
The analysis is limited to the BERT-base-uncased 12-layer model; generalizability to other models is not yet studied.
The study uses very simple linear probes; it is not explored if more complex probes would perform better.
future_direction: Study the impact of fine-tuning and context augmentation in the sub-layers using the sPWC/PWC dataset.
papers.abstract: In the era of high performing Large Language Models, researchers have widely acknowledged that contextual word representations are one of the key drivers in achieving top performances in downstream tasks. In this work, we investigate the degree of contextualization encoded in the fine-grained sub-layer representations of a Pre-trained Language Model (PLM) by empirical experiments using linear probes. Unlike previous work, we are particularly interested in identifying the strength of contextualization across PLM sub-layer representations (i.e. Self-Attention, Feed-Forward Activation and Output sub-layers). To identify the main contributions of sub-layers to contextualisation, we first extract the sub-layer representations of polysemous words in minimally different sentence pairs, and compare how these representations change through the forward pass of the PLM network. Second, by probing on a sense identification classification task, we try to empirically localize the strength of contextualization information encoded in these sub-layer representations. With these probing experiments, we also try to gain a better understanding of the influence of context length and context richness on the degree of contextualization. Our main conclusion is cautionary: BERT demonstrates a high degree of contextualization in the top sub-layers if the word in question is in a specific position in the sentence with a shorter context window, but this does not systematically generalize across different word positions and context sizes.

papers.title: Probing the Emergence of Cross-lingual Alignment during LLM Training
papers.research_question: How does cross-lingual alignment emerge during the pre-training of multilingual large language models?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates a strong correlation between cross-lingual neuron overlap and zero-shot transfer performance in multilingual LLMs, and reveals non-monotonic alignment dynamics during pre-training with drops in smaller models.
papers.conclusion: The study confirms that shared neurons encoding linguistic features are tightly connected to cross-lingual transfer ability, providing insights into multilingual pretraining dynamics.
papers.key_findings:
Neuron overlap for linguistic features increases during pre-training but experiences severe drops in smaller model scales like BLOOM560m and BLOOM1b1.
There is a statistically significant, strong correlation between neuron overlap and zero-shot cross-lingual transfer performance on tasks like POS tagging and XNLI.
Larger models (e.g., BLOOM1b7) show more monotonic growth in alignment, suggesting a scaling law effect.
Drops in alignment correspond to degradation in both in-language and cross-lingual performance.
The emergence of cross-lingual alignment is not steady and can pass through sub-optimal regions during training.
papers.limitation:
Focus on BLOOM checkpoints with large intervals, so findings might not apply to finer-grained training windows.
Only consider autoregressive models with the same objective and training dataset; varying these may result in different patterns.
Focus on alignment of languages seen during pretraining, leaving generalization to unseen languages for future research.
papers.abstract: Multilingual Large Language Models (LLMs) achieve remarkable levels of zero-shot cross-lingual transfer performance. We speculate that this is predicated on their ability to align languages without explicit supervision from parallel sentences. While representations of translationally equivalent sentences in different languages are known to be similar after convergence, however, it remains unclear how such cross-lingual alignment emerges during pre-training of LLMs. Our study leverages intrinsic probing techniques, which identify which subsets of neurons encode linguistic features, to correlate the degree of cross-lingual neuron overlap with the zero-shot cross-lingual transfer performance for a given model. In particular, we rely on checkpoints of BLOOM, a multilingual autoregressive LLM, across different training steps and model scales. We observe a high correlation between neuron overlap and downstream performance, which supports our hypothesis on the conditions leading to effective cross-lingual transfer. Interestingly, we also detect a degradation of both implicit alignment and multilingual abilities in certain phases of the pre-training process, providing new insights into the multilingual pretraining dynamics.

papers.title: What Makes Language Models Good-enough?
papers.research_question: What architectural features, specifically the number of layers and self-attention heads, make language models learn human-like good-enough language processing?
papers.core_contribution: This paper shows that language models with shallower depth and fewer attention heads can exhibit human-like good-enough language processing, indicating that deep architectures are not necessary for such performance.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that shallow transformer architectures can achieve human-like good-enough language processing, while the role of attention heads remains unclear.
papers.key_findings:
Models with shallower depth and fewer attention heads can learn good-enough language processing, similar to full models.
Increasing the number of layers from 8 to 12 does not significantly improve human-like good-enough performance.
The number of attention heads does not clearly contribute to models' good-enough performance, contradicting the hypothesis about working memory.
Human accuracy decreases with increased memory load, and models show a similar pattern, especially for items with correct no answers.
The GELP dataset effectively captures good-enough language processing phenomena in humans and models.
papers.limitation:
Model coverage is limited to BERT.
Use of templates in dataset creation may result in unnatural sentences.
Does not test whether models can perform in a human-like way in terms of both grammatical knowledge and good-enough language processing.
future_direction: Generalizing findings to other Transformer-based models such as GPT-2.
Testing whether models can learn the human-like balance between robust and heuristic language processing.
papers.abstract: Psycholinguistic research suggests that humans may build a representation of linguistic input that is 'good-enough' for the task at hand. This study examines what architectural features make language models learn human-like good-enough language processing. We focus on the number of layers and self-attention heads in Transformers. We create a good-enough language processing (GELP) evaluation dataset (7,680 examples), which is designed to test the effects of two plausibility types, eight construction types, and three degrees of memory cost on language processing. To annotate GELP, we first conduct a crowdsourcing experiment whose design follows prior psycholinguistic studies. Our model evaluation against the annotated GELP then reveals that the full model as well as models with fewer layers and/or self-attention heads exhibit a good-enough performance. This result suggests that models with shallower depth and fewer heads can learn good-enough language processing.

papers.title: Similarity of Sentence Representations in Multilingual LMs: Resolving Conflicting Literature and a Case Study of Baltic Languages
papers.research_question: How do multilingual language models internally represent different languages, and do they converge to a shared cross-lingual space?
papers.core_contribution: The paper resolves conflicting literature by showing that multilingual LMs project languages into a shared cross-lingual space when using mean-pooling and CKA/SVCCA, and finds that Baltic languages are part of this space.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that mean-pooling with SVCCA/CKA is optimal for cross-lingual representational similarity analysis, and while most languages share a cross-lingual space, Baltic languages are part of it.
papers.key_findings:
CLS-pooling with PWCCA gives divergent patterns, while mean-pooling with CKA/SVCCA shows convergence in cross-lingual similarity.
