To do so, we train an affine probe for each block in a frozen pretrained model, making it possible to decode every hidden state into a distribution over the vocabulary. Our method, the tuned lens, is a refinement of the earlier "logit lens" technique, which yielded useful insights but is often brittle. We test our method on various autoregressive language models with up to 20B parameters, showing it to be more predictive, reliable and unbiased than the logit lens. With causal experiments, we show the tuned lens uses similar features to the model itself. We also find the trajectory of latent predictions can be used to detect malicious inputs with high accuracy. All code needed to reproduce our results can be found at https://github.com/AlignmentResearch/tuned-lens.

papers.title: Rethinking the Value of Transformer Components
papers.research_question: How does each component (sub-layer) in a trained Transformer model contribute to the model performance, and can unimportant components be identified and utilized to improve training?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces two metrics (contribution in information flow and criticality in representation generalization) to evaluate the importance of individual Transformer components, finds that decoder self-attention layers are least important while decoder feed-forward layers are most important, and proposes a training strategy that rewinds unimportant components to initialization and fine-tunes to improve translation performance.
papers.conclusion: Different Transformer components are not equally important; decoder self-attention is least important and decoder feed-forward is most important. Rewinding unimportant components and fine-tuning can further improve translation performance.
papers.key_findings:
Decoder self-attention layers are least important, and decoder feed-forward layers are most important.
Components closer to the model input and output (lower encoder layers and higher decoder layers) are more important.
Upper encoder-attention layers in the decoder are more important than lower encoder-attention layers.
Lower dropout ratio and more training data lead to fewer unimportant components.
Rewinding unimportant components to initialization and then fine-tuning the model can improve translation performance.
future_direction: Designing better approaches to evaluate the impact of components (e.g., from the perspective of information flow).
Validating the findings on other neural machine translation architectures such as RNMT and ConvS2S.
papers.abstract: Transformer becomes the state-of-the-art translation model, while it is not well studied how each intermediate component contributes to the model performance, which poses significant challenges for designing optimal architectures. In this work, we bridge this gap by evaluating the impact of individual component (sub-layer) in trained Transformer models from different perspectives. Experimental results across language pairs, training strategies, and model capacities show that certain components are consistently more important than the others. We also report a number of interesting findings that might help humans better analyze, understand and improve Transformer models. Based on these observations, we further propose a new training strategy that can improves translation performance by distinguishing the unimportant components in training.

papers.title: Emergent effects of scaling on the functional hierarchies within large language models
papers.research_question: What is the functional hierarchy of abstraction across layers in LLMs, and how does it change with model scaling?
papers.core_contribution: Large language models exhibit functional hierarchies with abstraction increasing across layers, but scaling introduces deviations such as double representation peaks and anti-persistent fluctuations in attention mechanisms.
papers.conclusion: The study confirms functional hierarchies in LLMs but reveals emergent deviations with scaling, such as double representation peaks and layer coordination, complicating interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
Item-level semantics are most strongly represented in early layers (2-7), two-item relations in middle layers (8-12), and four-item analogies in later layers (10-15), consistent with an abstraction hierarchy.
Deep layers can represent narrow two-item relations from early in the context, suggesting information compression without meaningful abstraction.
In the large Llama-3.3-70b-Instruct model, representation of two-item relations and analogies shows two distinct peaks (layers 12-16 and 25-33), indicating fluctuations in abstraction level.
Adjacent layers in the large model exhibit anti-persistent fluctuations in attention outputs, with negative autocorrelation, suggesting coordinated specialization.
Buried concepts (target text followed by filler) are represented in deeper layers, showing that late layers capture global document-wide information.
papers.limitation:
The interpretation of the double-peak pattern and valley in large models is unclear and requires further work.
Analyses on grammar and syntax were inconclusive and not reported, limiting insights into syntactic processing.
future_direction: Study larger models to understand scaling effects further.
Investigate the mechanisms behind the double-peak representation and layer coordination.
Explore how late-layer representations can be used for steering and safety applications.
papers.abstract: Large language model (LLM) architectures are often described as functionally hierarchical: Early layers process syntax, middle layers begin to parse semantics, and late layers integrate information. The present work revisits these ideas. This research submits simple texts to an LLM (e.g., "A church and organ") and extracts the resulting activations. Then, for each layer, support vector machines and ridge regressions are fit to predict a text's label and thus examine whether a given layer encodes some information. Analyses using a small model (Llama-3.2-3b; 28 layers) partly bolster the common hierarchical perspective: Item-level semantics are most strongly represented early (layers 2-7), then two-item relations (layers 8-12), and then four-item analogies (layers 10-15). Afterward, the representation of items and simple relations gradually decreases in deeper layers that focus on more global information. However, several findings run counter to a steady hierarchy view: First, although deep layers can represent document-wide abstractions, deep layers also compress information from early portions of the context window without meaningful abstraction. Second, when examining a larger model (Llama-3.3-70b-Instruct), stark fluctuations in abstraction level appear: As depth increases, two-item relations and four-item analogies initially increase in their representation, then markedly decrease, and afterward increase again momentarily. This peculiar pattern consistently emerges across several experiments. Third, another emergent effect of scaling is coordination between the attention mechanisms of adjacent layers. Across multiple experiments using the larger model, adjacent layers fluctuate between what information they each specialize in representing. In sum, an abstraction hierarchy often manifests across layers, but large models also deviate from this structure in curious ways.

papers.title: FuxiTranyu: A Multilingual Large Language Model Trained with Balanced Data
papers.research_question: How to build a multilingual large language model with balanced data to mitigate performance discrepancies between high- and low-resource languages?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces FuxiTranyu, a multilingual LLM trained on balanced data, which shows competitive performance and more consistent multilingual representations compared to existing models.
papers.conclusion: FuxiTranyu is a strong open-source multilingual LLM, and balanced pre-training data is crucial for achieving consistent multilingual representations and performance.
papers.key_findings:
FuxiTranyu outperforms previous multilingual LLMs like BLOOM-7B1 and PolyLM-13B on several multilingual benchmarks.
Balanced pre-training data leads to more consistent multilingual representations across languages.
Neuron analysis reveals that deep layers are more language-specific and the importance of attention and MLP components varies across layers.
Languages with extremely limited resources (e.g., Bengali, Tamil) are allocated fewer neurons and perform poorly.
The model achieves high performance on summarization tasks, outperforming baseline models on XL-Sum.
papers.limitation:
Languages with extremely limited resources, such as Bengali and Tamil, are allocated with fewer neurons and perform poorly.
The model underperforms in some tasks (e.g., m-ARC, m-MMLU) due to limited training data for English.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated prowess in a wide range of tasks. However, many LLMs exhibit significant performance discrepancies between high- and low-resource languages. To mitigate this challenge, we present FuxiTranyu, an open-source multilingual LLM, which is designed to satisfy the need of the research community for balanced and high-performing multilingual capabilities. The base model, FuxiTranyu-8B, features 8 billion parameters and is trained from scratch on meticulously balanced multilingual data that contains 600 billion tokens covering 43 natural languages and 16 programming languages. We also develop two instruction-tuned models: FuxiTranyu-8B-SFT which is fine-tuned on a diverse multilingual instruction dataset, and FuxiTranyu-8B-DPO which is further refined with DPO on a preference dataset for enhanced alignment ability. Extensive experiments on a wide range of multilingual benchmarks demonstrate the competitive performance of FuxiTranyu against existing multilingual LLMs, e.g., BLOOM-7B, PolyLM-13B, and Mistral-7B-Instruct. Both neuron and representation interpretability analyses reveal that FuxiTranyu achieves consistent multilingual representations across languages. To promote further research into multilingual LLMs, we release both the base and instruction-tuned FuxiTranyu models together with 58 pre-training checkpoints at HuggingFace (see https://huggingface.co/TJUNLP/FuxiTranyu-8B) and Github (see https://github.com/tjunlp-lab/FuxiTranyu).

papers.title: Viewing Knowledge Transfer in Multilingual Machine Translation Through a Representational Lens
papers.research_question: What is the relationship between cross-lingual knowledge transfer and representational similarities in multilingual neural machine translation, and can we develop a better measure for transfer than translation quality alone?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces Representational Transfer Potential (RTP), a measure of knowledge transfer based on representational similarities between languages in multilingual machine translation, and proposes a novel training scheme with an auxiliary similarity loss that improves translation quality for low- and mid-resource languages.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that Representational Transfer Potential (RTP) is a better measure of knowledge transfer than translation quality alone, and that explicitly optimizing for language invariance using multi-parallel data improves translation for low-resource languages.
papers.key_findings:
Representational Transfer Potential (RTP) can measure both positive and negative transfer and is strongly correlated with changes in translation quality (BLEU), indicating that improvements are due to knowledge transfer and not just increased target data.
Multi-parallel overlap between languages is a highly predictive yet under-explored feature for transfer.
A training method that uses an auxiliary similarity loss to encourage language-invariant representations yields increased translation quality for low- and mid-resource languages across multiple data and model setups.
RTP can be used to identify suitable auxiliary transfer languages, with training on top RTP contributors leading to substantially better results than training on bottom contributors.
Dataset features (multi-parallel overlap, source subword overlap, vocabulary occupancy) are more predictive of representational similarity than linguistic features.
papers.limitation:
The analysis focuses on English-centric many-to-many and many-to-English models, which may limit the generalizability of the results to other multilingual settings.
The training data size (TED corpus) is relatively small compared to other datasets like OPUS-100, which may affect model performance.
papers.abstract: We argue that translation quality alone is not a sufficient metric for measuring knowledge transfer in multilingual neural machine translation. To support this claim, we introduce Representational Transfer Potential (RTP), which measures representational similarities between languages. We show that RTP can measure both positive and negative transfer (interference), and find that RTP is strongly correlated with changes in translation quality, indicating that transfer does occur. Furthermore, we investigate data and language characteristics that are relevant for transfer, and find that multi-parallel overlap is an important yet under-explored feature. Based on this, we develop a novel training scheme, which uses an auxiliary similarity loss that encourages representations to be more invariant across languages by taking advantage of multi-parallel data. We show that our method yields increased translation quality for low- and mid-resource languages across multiple data and model setups.

papers.title: Emergent World Representations: Exploring a Sequence Model Trained on a Synthetic Task
papers.research_question: Does a sequence model trained on a synthetic task (Othello game transcripts) learn an internal representation of the board state, and is that representation causal to its predictions?
papers.core_contribution: The paper provides evidence that a GPT model trained on Othello game transcripts learns a nonlinear internal representation of the board state, which is causally involved in its predictions. It introduces intervention techniques and latent saliency maps for interpretability.
papers.conclusion: The experiments provide evidence that Othello-GPT maintains a nonlinear internal representation of the game board state, which is causally linked to its predictions. The tools introduced (nonlinear probes, interventions, latent saliency maps) may prove useful for interpretability in natural language settings.
papers.key_findings:
Othello-GPT predicts legal moves with high accuracy, and this is not due to memorization.
Nonlinear probes can accurately decode the board state from internal activations, while linear probes perform poorly.
Intervention experiments show that the board representation is causal to the model's predictions.
Latent saliency maps reveal differences between models trained on synthetic vs. championship data, indicating different learned strategies.
The internal representation of the board state is nonlinear and emerges during training.
papers.limitation: Latent saliency maps only attribute to one tile when multiple tiles are involved in a move, which does not fully capture the Othello rule logic.
future_direction: Extend investigation to other, more complex games.
Compare strategies learned by a sequence model with those of a model trained with a priori knowledge of Othello.
Study how results generalize to natural language models.
papers.abstract: Language models show a surprising range of capabilities, but the source of their apparent competence is unclear. Do these networks just memorize a collection of surface statistics, or do they rely on internal representations of the process that generates the sequences they see? We investigate this question by applying a variant of the GPT model to the task of predicting legal moves in a simple board game, Othello. Although the network has no a priori knowledge of the game or its rules, we uncover evidence of an emergent nonlinear internal representation of the board state. Interventional experiments indicate this representation can be used to control the output of the network and create "latent saliency maps" that can help explain predictions in human terms.

papers.title: The Semantic Hub Hypothesis: Language Models Share Semantic Representations Across Languages and Modalities
papers.research_question: To what extent do language models learn and use a shared semantic representation space across different languages and modalities?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes the semantic hub hypothesis, which posits that language models learn a shared representation space across languages and modalities, and provides evidence through representation similarity and intervention experiments.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that language models learn a shared semantic representation space (the semantic hub) that is anchored by the dominant language and is causally involved in processing across languages and modalities.
papers.key_findings:
Model representations for semantically equivalent inputs in different languages are similar in intermediate layers.
The shared representation space is scaffolded by the model's dominant language (e.g., English) and can be interpreted via the logit lens.
This phenomenon extends to other data types: arithmetic expressions, code, images, and audio.
Interventions in the shared space using the dominant language affect model outputs in other data types, indicating causal usage.
The shared space is not just a byproduct but actively used during processing.
papers.limitation:
Chameleon-7B cannot answer more sophisticated reasoning questions about images, such as asking for a country flag or spatial relationships, even without interventions.
The logit lens analysis for audio is a lower bound because many words in labels (e.g., prepositions) are unlikely to be represented in the audio hidden states.
future_direction: Future work aimed at better controlling models using insights from the semantic hub hypothesis.
papers.abstract: Modern language models can process inputs across diverse languages and modalities. We hypothesize that models acquire this capability through learning a shared representation space across heterogeneous data types (e.g., different languages and modalities), which places semantically similar inputs near one another, even if they are from different modalities/languages. We term this the semantic hub hypothesis, following the hub-and-spoke model from neuroscience (Patterson et al., 2007) which posits that semantic knowledge in the human brain is organized through a transmodal semantic "hub" which integrates information from various modality-specific "spokes" regions. We first show that model representations for semantically equivalent inputs in different languages are similar in the intermediate layers, and that this space can be interpreted using the model's dominant pretraining language via the logit lens. This tendency extends to other data types, including arithmetic expressions, code, and visual/audio inputs. Interventions in the shared representation space in one data type also predictably affect model outputs in other data types, suggesting that this shared representations space is not simply a vestigial byproduct of large-scale training on broad data, but something that is actively utilized by the model during input processing.

papers.title: exBERT: A Visual Analysis Tool to Explore Learned Representations in Transformers Models
papers.research_question: How to interactively explore and understand what attention heads in transformer models have learned, specifically in BERT, by combining attention visualization with nearest neighbor search on annotated corpora.
papers.core_contribution: Introduces EXBERT, an interactive visualization tool that uses linguistic annotations, interactive masking, and nearest neighbor search to explore and explain learned representations and attention mechanisms in transformer models.
papers.conclusion: EXBERT is an interactive visualization tool that uses linguistic annotations, interactive masking, and nearest neighbor search to reveal intelligible structure in learned representations of transformer models, demonstrated with BERT on the Wizard of Oz corpus.
papers.key_findings:
At early layers (e.g., layer 1), masked token embeddings show similarity to common tokens like punctuation and determinants, with no meaningful linguistic information encoded.
As layers progress, more part-of-speech information is added; by layer 6, BERT becomes confident that a masked token is a verb, refining this estimation in later layers.
Complex dependencies such as direct object (DOBJ) are detected in early-middle layers but rely on a combination of multiple attention heads, not individual heads.
Positional heads attend to succeeding or preceding tokens and encode linguistic information about the attended-to word, such as part-of-speech and dependency relations.
EXBERT enables interactive exploration of how attention heads contribute to encoding linguistic features in token embeddings through nearest neighbor search on annotated corpora.
papers.abstract: Large language models can produce powerful contextual representations that lead to improvements across many NLP tasks. Since these models are typically guided by a sequence of learned self attention mechanisms and may comprise undesired inductive biases, it is paramount to be able to explore what the attention has learned. While static analyses of these models lead to targeted insights, interactive tools are more dynamic and can help humans better gain an intuition for the model-internal reasoning process. We present exBERT, an interactive tool named after the popular BERT language model, that provides insights into the meaning of the contextual representations by matching a human-specified input to similar contexts in a large annotated dataset. By aggregating the annotations of the matching similar contexts, exBERT helps intuitively explain what each attention-head has learned.

papers.title: Exploring Cross-lingual Latent Transplantation: Mutual Opportunities and Open Challenges
papers.research_question: Can LLMs leverage both their robust capabilities (in English) and their multilingual knowledge (in non-English languages) during inference to further unlock their multilingual potential?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Cross-lingual Latent Transplantation (X Transplant), a probing framework that transplants latent activations across languages at inference time to unlock multilingual and cultural knowledge in LLMs, revealing underutilized potential.
papers.conclusion: The analysis offers a new lens for advancing cross-lingual interactions and better leveraging models' internalized multilingual knowledge.
papers.key_findings:
X Transplant has mutually beneficial effects on multilingual capability and cultural adaptability, especially for low-resource languages and cultures.
Attention modules play a pivotal role in supporting multilingual understanding, while feed-forward modules are more adept at capturing culture-specific knowledge.
The upper-bound performance of X Transplant reveals a significant underutilization of current LLMs' multilingual potential.
English boosts multilingual capability, while non-English improves cultural adaptability.
papers.abstract: Current large language models (LLMs) often exhibit imbalances in multilingual capabilities and cultural adaptability, largely attributed to their English-centric pre-training data. In this paper, we introduce and investigate a cross-lingual latent transplantation (XTransplant) framework, which aims to further exploit the model's internalized multilingual knowledge during inference and examine its effects on the multilingual capability and cultural adaptability of LLMs. XTransplant framework enables models to harness the complementary strengths of both English and non-English resources by transplanting latent activations across languages. Through extensive analysis, we empirically demonstrate that XTransplant, a form of cross-lingual interaction, has mutually beneficial effects on the multilingual capability and cultural adaptability of LLMs, particularly for low-resource languages and cultures. We further reveal that attention modules play a pivotal role in supporting multilingual understanding, while feed-forward modules are more adept at capturing culture-specific knowledge. In addition, we conduct in-depth analysis of XTransplant's stability, effectiveness, and generalizability. By probing the upper bound performance of XTransplant, we expose the considerable underutilization of current LLMs' multilingual potential-a challenge that remains open. We hope our analysis offers a new lens for advancing cross-lingual interactions and better leveraging models' internalized multilingual knowledge.

papers.title: Word Meanings in Transformer Language Models
papers.research_question: How are word meanings represented in transformer language models? Specifically, do transformer models use a lexical store that encodes semantic information in static token embeddings?
papers.core_contribution: The static token embeddings in transformer language models encode a wide variety of semantic information, supporting the idea that LLMs use a lexical store for word meanings and ruling out meaning eliminativist hypotheses.
papers.conclusion: Static embeddings in transformer models store meaningful semantic information, not just syntactic and surface-level features, indicating LLMs require a lexical store of semantic information for understanding text.
papers.key_findings:
Manual inspection of k-means clusters from RoBERTa-base static embeddings reveals many clusters organized by semantic categories (e.g., colors, tools, medical terms).
Quantitative analysis shows clusters are sensitive to psycholinguistic attributes (valence, concreteness, iconicity, taboo, age of acquisition), indicating semantic information is encoded.
The findings rule out meaning eliminativist hypotheses that static embeddings contain little semantic information.
The static embedding space encodes both taxonomic and thematic relations among words.
Some clusters capture worldly information (e.g., political names, sports teams) in addition to semantic features.
papers.limitation:
The iconicity findings are limited, with only 9 sensitive clusters and no clear iconicity-related features upon manual inspection; iconicity may correlate with surface features like syllable count.
The taboo attribute list is small (1,085 tokens), leading to sampling errors and a small number of sensitive clusters.
Clusters sensitive to an attribute might be sensitive to correlative properties rather than the attribute itself.
future_direction: Using alternative embeddings and clustering algorithms (e.g., variations of the EM algorithm).
Using alternative null hypotheses in statistical tests.
Considering subsets of corpora partitioned by source classifications (e.g., cultural biases, sub-populations, settings) to test for idiosyncratic meanings.
papers.abstract: We investigate how word meanings are represented in the transformer language models. Specifically, we focus on whether transformer models employ something analogous to a lexical store - where each word has an entry that contains semantic information. To do this, we extracted the token embedding space of RoBERTa-base and k-means clustered it into 200 clusters. In our first study, we then manually inspected the resultant clusters to consider whether they are sensitive to semantic information. In our second study, we tested whether the clusters are sensitive to five psycholinguistic measures: valence, concreteness, iconicity, taboo, and age of acquisition. Overall, our findings were very positive - there is a wide variety of semantic information encoded within the token embedding space. This serves to rule out certain "meaning eliminativist" hypotheses about how transformer LLMs process semantic information.

papers.title: Label Words are Anchors: An Information Flow Perspective for Understanding In-Context Learning
papers.research_question: How does in-context learning (ICL) work in large language models, specifically what is the role of label words in the information flow?
papers.core_contribution: Label words serve as anchors in in-context learning: they aggregate information from demonstrations in shallow layers and provide reference for predictions in deep layers.
papers.conclusion: Label words function as anchors in ICL, aggregating and distributing task-relevant information; this understanding enables improvements in accuracy, efficiency, and interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
Label words aggregate information from demonstration examples in shallow transformer layers.
The model extracts information from label words in deep layers to form the final prediction.
Anchor re-weighting, which adjusts the significance of label words, improves ICL accuracy by an average of 16.7%.
Compressing demonstrations to anchor hidden states (Hiddenanchor) speeds up inference by up to 1.8× with minimal performance loss.
ICL errors can be diagnosed by analyzing distances between anchor key vectors, which correlate with category confusion.
papers.limitation:
The study is limited to classification tasks and does not explore generative tasks.
Due to hardware constraints, models are limited to up to 6 billion parameters, leaving larger-scale models unexplored.
The hypothesis is only examined in conventional ICL paradigms, not in others like chain-of-thought prompting.
future_direction: Replicating the study with larger-scale models.
Exploring other ICL paradigms such as chain-of-thought prompting.
papers.abstract: In-context learning (ICL) emerges as a promising capability of large language models (LLMs) by providing them with demonstration examples to perform diverse tasks. However, the underlying mechanism of how LLMs learn from the provided context remains under-explored. In this paper, we investigate the working mechanism of ICL through an information flow lens. Our findings reveal that label words in the demonstration examples function as anchors: (1) semantic information aggregates into label word representations during the shallow computation layers' processing; (2) the consolidated information in label words serves as a reference for LLMs' final predictions. Based on these insights, we introduce an anchor re-weighting method to improve ICL performance, a demonstration compression technique to expedite inference, and an analysis framework for diagnosing ICL errors in GPT2-XL. The promising applications of our findings again validate the uncovered ICL working mechanism and pave the way for future studies.

papers.title: How Programming Concepts and Neurons Are Shared in Code Language Models
papers.research_question: How do code language models represent multiple programming languages and English in their concept space? Specifically, do they use a pivot language, and can we identify language-specific neurons?
papers.core_contribution: The paper investigates how code language models represent programming languages and English, finding that English and certain PLs (like C#) are central in the concept space, and that language-specific neurons exist but are challenging to identify for highly aligned PLs.
papers.conclusion: Our findings deepen our understanding of LLMs’ inner workings in the context of PLs and provide valuable insights for interpretability in code-related tasks.
papers.key_findings:
English and PL keywords appear in intermediate layers with high probabilities in the second half of the layers.
C# is highly aligned with other PLs in the model's concept space.
Language-specific neurons are concentrated in bottom layers, while PL-exclusive neurons are in top layers.
For highly aligned PLs (like C# and Java), identifying language-specific neurons is challenging.
The model's concept space is closer to English and assigns high probabilities to English tokens in intermediate layers during translation tasks.
papers.limitation:
The super-parallel dataset is limited to seven languages due to source constraints.
Using keywords to interpret latent embeddings may not be precise because some PL keywords lack direct English meanings or map to multiple tokens.
The analysis is limited to Llama-based architectures; exploring other architectures is needed for broader validation.
papers.abstract: Several studies have explored the mechanisms of large language models (LLMs) in coding tasks, but most have focused on programming languages (PLs) in a monolingual setting. In this paper, we investigate the relationship between multiple PLs and English in the concept space of LLMs. We perform a few-shot translation task on 21 PL pairs using two Llama-based models. By decoding the embeddings of intermediate layers during this task, we observe that the concept space is closer to English (including PL keywords) and assigns high probabilities to English tokens in the second half of the intermediate layers. We analyze neuron activations for 11 PLs and English, finding that while language-specific neurons are primarily concentrated in the bottom layers, those exclusive to each PL tend to appear in the top layers. For PLs that are highly aligned with multiple other PLs, identifying language-specific neurons is not feasible. These PLs also tend to have a larger keyword set than other PLs and are closer to the model's concept space regardless of the input/output PL in the translation task. Our findings provide insights into how LLMs internally represent PLs, revealing structural patterns in the model's concept space. Code is available at https://github.com/cisnlp/code-specific-neurons.

papers.title: Causal Analysis of Syntactic Agreement Neurons in Multilingual Language Models
papers.research_question: How and where do multilingual language models encode syntactic agreement? Are neurons shared across languages and structures?
papers.core_contribution: This paper extends causal probing to multilingual language models, finding two distinct layer-wise effect patterns for syntactic agreement depending on distance, significant neuron overlap across languages in autoregressive multilingual models but not masked language models, and that behavioral analyses underestimate masked language models' sensitivity to syntax.
papers.conclusion: Causal probing reveals distinct mechanisms for short- and long-range syntactic agreement in multilingual models, with autoregressive models showing more cross-lingual neuron sharing than masked models, and suggests that models encode syntax similarly across languages but with language-specific neurons.
papers.key_findings:
Two distinct layer-wise effect patterns for syntactic agreement: one for short-range (adjacent subject-verb) and one for long-range (separated by other tokens).
Neurons are shared across syntactic structures but not with semantic baselines, indicating abstract syntactic agreement encoding.
In autoregressive language models (XGLM), there is significant neuron overlap across languages, but in masked language models (mBERT), neurons are rarely shared across languages.
Neuron sparsity differs across structures (more sparse for short-range agreement) but not across languages.
Behavioral analyses likely underestimate how sensitive masked language models are to syntactic information because negative interference from other neurons masks strong syntax-sensitive neurons.
papers.limitation:
Limited to stimuli where subjects and verbs are single tokens, restricting the range of words and languages that can be studied.
Probing individual neurons may oversimplify because complex phenomena like syntactic agreement are likely encoded in sets of neurons.
future_direction: Developing methods for multi-token interventions and variable-length sequences.
Probing multiple neurons simultaneously to causally implicate model regions rather than individual components.
Investigating redundantly encoded syntactic information across neurons.
papers.abstract: Structural probing work has found evidence for latent syntactic information in pre-trained language models. However, much of this analysis has focused on monolingual models, and analyses of multilingual models have employed correlational methods that are confounded by the choice of probing tasks. In this study, we causally probe multilingual language models (XGLM and multilingual BERT) as well as monolingual BERT-based models across various languages; we do this by performing counterfactual perturbations on neuron activations and observing the effect on models' subject-verb agreement probabilities. We observe where in the model and to what extent syntactic agreement is encoded in each language. We find significant neuron overlap across languages in autoregressive multilingual language models, but not masked language models. We also find two distinct layer-wise effect patterns and two distinct sets of neurons used for syntactic agreement, depending on whether the subject and verb are separated by other tokens. Finally, we find that behavioral analyses of language models are likely underestimating how sensitive masked language models are to syntactic information.

papers.title: MALT: Mechanistic Ablation of Lossy Translation in LLMs for a Low-Resource Language: Urdu
papers.research_question: How do LLMs process low-resource languages, and can their performance be improved by mechanistically removing lossy translation features?
papers.core_contribution: LLMs have coherent internal English responses for low-resource language inputs, but lossy translation features in final layers degrade output. Mechanistically ablating these features and using a separate translation model significantly improves performance while preserving cultural nuances.
papers.conclusion: LLMs understand low-resource languages well but generate poorly due to lossy translation features. MALT improves performance by ablating these features and using external translation, preserving cultural context, but further work is needed.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs generate more coherent internal latent responses in English for low-resource language inputs compared to their direct outputs.
Translation features in the final layers of LLMs are lossy for low-resource languages, leading to poor generation quality.
Mechanistically ablating these translation features and using a separate machine translation model significantly improves response quality.
The proposed MALT method preserves cultural nuances of the input language.
Performance improvement varies between models, with Llama-3.2-3b showing greater gains than Gemma-2-2b.
papers.limitation:
Implemented on smaller LLMs; for larger LLMs, translation features may be more distributed, making ablation complex.
Generalization to other low-resource languages is untested.
Errors may stem from ablation of non-translation features or from LLM's poor understanding of input.
Focuses on generating detailed answers, not other formats like conversations or few-shot prompting.
Performance difference between models (e.g., Llama-3.2-3b vs. Gemma-2-2b) requires further investigation.
Cultural nuance preservation is indicated but not quantitatively verified.
future_direction: Refine methods and apply to larger LLMs.
Explore more precise ablation techniques to avoid affecting non-translation features.
Investigate generalization to other low-resource languages.
papers.abstract: LLMs are predominantly trained on English data, which leads to a significant drop in performance on low-resource languages. Understanding how LLMs handle these languages is crucial for improving their effectiveness. This study focuses on Urdu as a use case for exploring the challenges faced by LLMs in processing low-resource languages. LLMs primarily reason in English when prompted in another language, with the final layers acting as translators to convert the English response into the target language. This study finds that even for low-resource languages, the internal latent response of LLMs in English is quite coherent; however, the translation features are lossy and result in poor translations, leading to reduced performance. By mechanistically removing these translation features and using a separate translation model to translate the internal latent response of LLM, the performance of LLMs improves significantly while also preserving the cultural nuances of the input in low-resource languages.

papers.title: Low-Dimensional Structure in the Space of Language Representations is Reflected in Brain Responses
papers.research_question: How related are the representations learned by neural language models, translation models, and language tagging tasks? Does the low-dimensional structure of these representations correspond to brain responses during language processing?
papers.core_contribution: The paper reveals a low-dimensional structure in the space of language representations and shows that this structure can predict how well each representation maps to human brain responses to natural language, suggesting it captures part of the brain's natural language representation hierarchy.
papers.conclusion: The low-dimensional structure in language representations reflects the brain's natural language processing hierarchy, suggesting that the embedding captures some part of the brain's representation structure.
papers.key_findings:
A low-dimensional structure exists in the space of language representations, with the first MDS dimension capturing a progression from word embeddings to syntactic/semantic tasks to next-word embeddings.
The representation embeddings can predict fMRI encoding model performance, indicating a link between the representation space and brain responses.
Projecting the first MDS dimension onto the brain recovers known language processing hierarchies, with early auditory cortex explained by lower-level features and higher-order areas by later layers.
Most pairs of representations can be correctly matched to their brain response patterns using the representation embeddings.
The low-dimensional structure is consistent across different language models and translation models.
papers.limitation: Negative discriminability scores for some representation pairs, possibly due to disconnect between task affinities and brain representations, e.g., for GloVe next-word embedding.
papers.abstract: How related are the representations learned by neural language models, translation models, and language tagging tasks? We answer this question by adapting an encoder-decoder transfer learning method from computer vision to investigate the structure among 100 different feature spaces extracted from hidden representations of various networks trained on language tasks. This method reveals a low-dimensional structure where language models and translation models smoothly interpolate between word embeddings, syntactic and semantic tasks, and future word embeddings. We call this low-dimensional structure a language representation embedding because it encodes the relationships between representations needed to process language for a variety of NLP tasks. We find that this representation embedding can predict how well each individual feature space maps to human brain responses to natural language stimuli recorded using fMRI. Additionally, we find that the principal dimension of this structure can be used to create a metric which highlights the brain's natural language processing hierarchy. This suggests that the embedding captures some part of the brain's natural language representation structure.

papers.title: Discovering Latent Concepts Learned in BERT
papers.research_question: What latent concepts exist in the pre-trained BERT model, how do the discovered latent concepts align or diverge from classical linguistic hierarchy, and how do the latent concepts evolve across layers?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces an unsupervised method to discover and analyze latent concepts learned in BERT, and releases a novel multi-facet hierarchical concept dataset (BCN).
papers.conclusion: The work provides a comprehensive analysis of latent concepts in BERT and releases a novel BERT-centric concept dataset (BCN) that facilitates future interpretation studies and serves as an annotated resource.
papers.key_findings:
BERT learns novel concepts (e.g., animal categories, demographic groups) that do not strictly adhere to pre-defined linguistic categories.
Many latent concepts are based on multiple properties (e.g., semantics, syntax, morphology).
Lower layers dominate in learning shallow lexical concepts, while higher layers learn semantic relations.
The discovered latent concepts highlight potential biases learned in the model (e.g., gender and demographic associations).
Concepts learned at higher layers are more aligned with linguistically motivated concepts compared to lower layers.
papers.limitation:
The diversity of observed concepts is limited by the dataset and clustering constraints (memory and algorithm).
Only the final layer of BERT was manually annotated due to annotation cost.
The method is limited to word-level concepts; phrase-level concepts are not explored.
future_direction: Increase diversity of concepts by working around memory and algorithm constraints.
Explore phrase-level concepts.
Incorporate principal component analysis for more controlled analysis.
papers.abstract: A large number of studies that analyze deep neural network models and their ability to encode various linguistic and non-linguistic concepts provide an interpretation of the inner mechanics of these models. The scope of the analyses is limited to pre-defined concepts that reinforce the traditional linguistic knowledge and do not reflect on how novel concepts are learned by the model. We address this limitation by discovering and analyzing latent concepts learned in neural network models in an unsupervised fashion and provide interpretations from the model's perspective. In this work, we study: i) what latent concepts exist in the pre-trained BERT model, ii) how the discovered latent concepts align or diverge from classical linguistic hierarchy and iii) how the latent concepts evolve across layers. Our findings show: i) a model learns novel concepts (e.g. animal categories and demographic groups), which do not strictly adhere to any pre-defined categorization (e.g. POS, semantic tags), ii) several latent concepts are based on multiple properties which may include semantics, syntax, and morphology, iii) the lower layers in the model dominate in learning shallow lexical concepts while the higher layers learn semantic relations and iv) the discovered latent concepts highlight potential biases learned in the model. We also release a novel BERT ConceptNet dataset (BCN) consisting of 174 concept labels and 1M annotated instances.

papers.title: On the Sub-layer Functionalities of Transformer Decoder
papers.research_question: How do source and target information evolve within the Transformer decoder layer-by-layer and module-by-module? How does the Source Exploitation Module (SEM) exploit source information in different layers? How does the Information Fusion Module (IFM) fuse source and target information?
papers.core_contribution: This paper analyzes the functionalities of sub-layers within the Transformer decoder for neural machine translation, introducing a universal probing scheme. A key finding is that the residual feed-forward module can be removed with minimal performance loss, significantly boosting speed.
papers.conclusion: The analysis provides insights into how the Transformer decoder leverages source and target information across layers and modules. These findings can inspire architectural improvements, such as incorporating external alignment signals, exploring different sub-layer stacking orders, and pruning redundant components for efficiency.
papers.key_findings:
The Source Exploitation Module (SEM) guides the representation evolution of both source and target information within the decoder.
Higher-layer SEMs focus on word alignment, while lower-layer SEMs gather broader source context.
The Target Exploitation Module (TEM) is critical for building word alignments in SEM, but its stacking order with SEM is not essential.
The Information Fusion Module (IFM) can be simplified to a single Add&Norm operation, removing the feed-forward network, with minimal translation quality loss and significant speed improvements.
The simplified decoder (without feed-forward modules) achieves comparable BLEU scores while increasing training and inference speed by 11-14% for Base models and up to 50% for inference on some tasks.
future_direction: Improving word alignment of higher SEMs by incorporating external alignment signals.
Exploring the stacking order of SEM, TEM and IFM sub-layers for more effective information transformation.
Applying the analysis methods to other sequence-to-sequence tasks like summarization and grammar error correction.
Exploring other architectures such as RNMT, ConvS2S, or document-level NMT.
papers.abstract: There have been significant efforts to interpret the encoder of Transformer-based encoderdecoder architectures for neural machine translation (NMT); meanwhile, the decoder remains largely unexamined despite its critical role. During translation, the decoder must predict output tokens by considering both the source-language text from the encoder and the target-language prefix produced in previous steps. In this work, we study how Transformerbased decoders leverage information from the source and target languages -developing a universal probe task to assess how information is propagated through each module of each decoder layer. We perform extensive experiments on three major translation datasets (WMT En-De, En-Fr, and En-Zh). Our analysis provides insight on when and where decoders leverage different sources. Based on these insights, we demonstrate that the residual feed-forward module in each Transformer decoder layer can be dropped with minimal loss of performance -a significant reduction in computation and number of parameters, and consequently a significant boost to both training and inference speed.

papers.title: Why transformers are obviously good models of language
papers.research_question: Why are transformers effective models of language, and how do they align with theoretical perspectives on language?
papers.core_contribution: The paper argues that transformers are good models of language because their architecture, such as word embeddings and attention mechanisms, aligns with cognitive linguistic theories like prototype theory and construction grammar.
papers.conclusion: Transformers are effective models of language, and their alignment with certain linguistic theories suggests that these theories, such as those from cognitive linguistics, are correct.
papers.key_findings:
Word embeddings in transformers represent prototypical meanings of words, similar to Rosch's prototype theory.
Contextualized word meanings are constructed through self-attention layers, updating prototypes based on context.
Transformers can handle syntax and top-down processing via attention heads and skip connections, analogous to construction grammar.
Transformers lack a bias for local dependencies, allowing them to learn rare long-distance dependencies effectively.
The empirical success of transformers supports cognitive linguistic approaches over traditional syntactic theories.
papers.limitation:
Transformers assert false facts with the same degree of authority as true information.
Transformers have myopia in social contexts, such as not remembering past interactions in chatbots.
papers.abstract: Nobody knows how language works, but many theories abound. Transformers are a class of neural networks that process language automatically with more success than alternatives, both those based on neural computations and those that rely on other (e.g. more symbolic) mechanisms. Here, I highlight direct connections between the transformer architecture and certain theoretical perspectives on language. The empirical success of transformers relative to alternative models provides circumstantial evidence that the linguistic approaches that transformers embody should be, at least, evaluated with greater scrutiny by the linguistics community and, at best, considered to be the currently best available theories.

papers.title: Jump to Conclusions: Short-Cutting Transformers With Linear Transformations
papers.research_question: Is there a more accurate way to cast hidden representations into final representation substitutes than interpreting them as they are (identity mapping)?
papers.core_contribution: A simple method using linear transformations to cast hidden representations to final-layer substitutes, which improves interpretability and efficiency.
papers.conclusion: Linear mappings provide a simple and effective way to enhance the utilization of hidden representations for interpretability and efficiency, revealing linear structure in transformer components.
papers.key_findings:
Linear mappings (mat) consistently outperform identity mapping (id) in approximating future hidden representations and final predictions.
The method allows accurate prediction estimation from early layers, showing that models often predict the final output early.
The learned linear mappings generalize well across different model scales and data distributions.
When applied to early exiting, the method saves additional layers (e.g., 7.9% for GPT-2, 5.4% for BERT) while retaining 95% accuracy.
Attention sub-modules are the most tolerant to linear approximation compared to FFN and layer normalization.
papers.limitation:
Focuses only on linear transformations, leaving affine or non-linear transformations for future work.
Does not elucidate the reason for the linear structure observed in transformer inference.
Only considers post-hoc interpretability (analyzing trained models without changing weights).
Experiments are conducted only on English data.
future_direction: Exploring affine or non-linear transformations for casting hidden representations.
Integrating linear mappings into model training rather than only post-hoc analysis.
Breaking the computation into parallel tasks to improve efficiency.
Comparing the method with other approaches like Belrose et al. (2023).
Investigating the reasons for the linear structure in transformer components.
papers.abstract: Transformer-based language models create hidden representations of their inputs at every layer, but only use final-layer representations for prediction. This obscures the internal decision-making process of the model and the utility of its intermediate representations. One way to elucidate this is to cast the hidden representations as final representations, bypassing the transformer computation in-between. In this work, we suggest a simple method for such casting, using linear transformations. This approximation far exceeds the prevailing practice of inspecting hidden representations from all layers, in the space of the final layer. Moreover, in the context of language modeling, our method produces more accurate predictions from hidden layers, across various model scales, architectures, and data distributions. This allows "peeking" into intermediate representations, showing that GPT-2 and BERT often predict the final output already in early layers. We then demonstrate the practicality of our method to recent early exit strategies, showing that when aiming, for example, at retention of 95% accuracy, our approach saves additional 7.9% layers for GPT-2 and 5.4% layers for BERT. Last, we extend our method to linearly approximate sub-modules, finding that attention is most tolerant to this change. Our code and learned mappings are publicly available at https://github.com/sashayd/mat.

papers.title: Post-hoc analysis of Arabic transformer models
papers.research_question: How is linguistic information encoded in transformer models trained on different Arabic dialects? Specifically, how do these models capture word morphology and dialectal nuances?
papers.core_contribution: This paper presents a post-hoc analysis of Arabic transformer models, revealing how linguistic information (morphology and dialect) is encoded across layers and neurons, and showing that models trained only on Modern Standard Arabic fail to capture dialectal nuances.
papers.conclusion: The analysis reveals how Arabic transformer models encode linguistic information, with morphology in lower/middle layers and dialect in higher layers, and shows that MSA-trained models lack dialectal understanding.
papers.key_findings:
Word morphology is captured in lower and middle layers of the transformer models.
Dialect identification, requiring long-range context, is captured in higher layers.
Models trained only on Modern Standard Arabic fail to capture dialectal nuances.
Neurons in the embedding layer are polysemous, while neurons in middle layers are specialized for specific properties.
Salient neurons for linguistic tasks are distributed across the network, with embedding and final layers contributing the most.
papers.limitation: For the DIA task, overfitting occurs when supervised data is insufficient, as classifiers with large contextualized vectors tend to overfit.
future_direction: Expand analysis to include more tasks.
Explore related languages such as Semitic, Germanic, or Latin languages.
papers.abstract: Arabic is a Semitic language which is widely spoken with many dialects. Given the success of pre-trained language models, many transformer models trained on Arabic and its dialects have surfaced. While there have been an extrinsic evaluation of these models with respect to downstream NLP tasks, no work has been carried out to analyze and compare their internal representations. We probe how linguistic information is encoded in the transformer models, trained on different Arabic dialects. We perform a layer and neuron analysis on the models using morphological tagging tasks for different dialects of Arabic and a dialectal identification task. Our analysis enlightens interesting findings such as: i) word morphology is learned at the lower and middle layers, ii) while syntactic dependencies are predominantly captured at the higher layers, iii) despite a large overlap in their vocabulary, the MSA-based models fail to capture the nuances of Arabic dialects, iv) we found that neurons in embedding layers are polysemous in nature, while the neurons in middle layers are exclusive to specific properties

papers.title: Multilingual Probing of Deep Pre-Trained Contextual Encoders
papers.research_question: What linguistic information do multilingual pre-trained contextual encoders retain, and how does this information vary across languages, encoders, and tasks?
papers.core_contribution: This paper provides a comprehensive multilingual evaluation of pre-trained encoders using probing tasks, revealing that recurrent architectures (ELMo) better retain lower-level linguistic information than self-attentive ones (BERT, XLM), and that cross-lingual training (XLM) leads to a loss of language-specific linguistic details.
papers.conclusion: Probing is a useful method for comparing encoders across languages, and the choice of encoder architecture and training objective significantly affects what linguistic information is retained, with cross-lingual models sacrificing language-specific details.
papers.key_findings:
Recurrent architectures (ELMo) retain lower-level linguistic phenomena (e.g., sentence length, word count) better than self-attentive architectures (BERT, XLM).
XLM performs worse on most probing tasks compared to BERT and ELMo, likely due to its cross-lingual training objective causing a loss of language-specific information.
For semantic tasks, the performance gap between recurrent and self-attentive architectures is smaller.
Language-specific differences exist; for example, French and Spanish perform better on subject and object number tasks due to morphological marking.
The results do not indicate that English is better represented in the multilingual models than the other languages studied.
papers.limitation:
Use of non-gold-standard dependency parses for some languages may introduce inaccuracies in the probing data.
The probing tasks are limited and do not include many truly semantic tasks.
future_direction: Designing more semantic-level probing tasks, possibly using cross-lingual semantic resources like the Parallel Meaning Bank.
Extending the evaluation to more languages and tasks.
papers.abstract: Encoders that generate representations based on context have, in recent years, benefited from adaptations that allow for pre-training on large text corpora. Earlier work on evaluating fixed-length sentence representations has included the use of ‘probing’ tasks, that use diagnostic classifiers to attempt to quantify the extent to which these encoders capture specific linguistic phenomena. The principle of probing has also resulted in extended evaluations that include relatively newer word-level pre-trained encoders. We build on probing tasks established in the literature and comprehensively evaluate and analyse – from a typological perspective amongst others – multilingual variants of existing encoders on probing datasets constructed for 6 non-English languages. Specifically, we probe each layer of a multiple monolingual RNN-based ELMo models, the transformer-based BERT’s cased and uncased multilingual variants, and a variant of BERT that uses a cross-lingual modelling scheme (XLM).

papers.title: Tracing the Roots of Facts in Multilingual Language Models: Independent, Shared, and Transferred Knowledge
papers.research_question: This paper investigates how multilingual language models acquire and represent factual knowledge across languages, specifically examining the factors affecting probing performance, whether fact representations are shared or independent across languages, and how cross-lingual representations are formed.
papers.core_contribution: The paper establishes methods for distinguishing three types of fact representations in multilingual language models (language-independent, cross-lingual shared, and cross-lingual transferred) and reveals the challenges in cross-lingual factual knowledge transfer.
papers.conclusion: Our research establishes the groundwork for further studies in understanding cross-lingual factual knowledge representation and highlights the challenges in achieving effective cross-lingual transfer of factual knowledge from high-resource to low-resource languages in ML-LMs.
papers.key_findings:
Factual probing performance across languages shows moderate correlation with training data volume and strong negative correlation with mask token count.
There are localized knowledge sharing patterns among geographically proximate languages.
ML-LMs exhibit both language-independent and cross-lingual fact representations, even for the same fact.
Active fact neurons in low-resource languages are more active and distributed in shallow layers compared to high-resource languages.
Cross-lingual transfer of factual knowledge does occur but is limited, and many correctly predicted facts in low-resource languages can be attributed to simple inference patterns rather than true transfer.
papers.limitation: The study is limited to encoder-based models (mBERT and XLM-R) and may not generalize to large decoder-based multilingual models.
future_direction: Enhance the cross-lingual fact representation learning in ML-LMs.
Develop a more precise factual probing dataset.
papers.abstract: Acquiring factual knowledge for language models (LMs) in low-resource languages poses a serious challenge, thus resorting to cross-lingual transfer in multilingual LMs (ML-LMs).In this study, we ask how ML-LMs acquire and represent factual knowledge.Using the multilingual factual knowledge probing dataset, mLAMA, we first conducted a neuron investigation of ML-LMs (specifically, multilingual BERT).We then traced the roots of facts back to the knowledge source (Wikipedia) to identify the ways in which ML-LMs acquire specific facts.We finally identified three patterns of acquiring and representing facts in ML-LMs: languageindependent, cross-lingual shared and transferred, and devised methods for differentiating them.Our findings highlight the challenge of maintaining consistent factual knowledge across languages, underscoring the need for better fact representation learning in ML-LMs. 1

papers.title: On the Linguistic Representational Power of Neural Machine Translation\n Models
papers.research_question: What linguistic information (morphology, syntax, semantics) is captured by neural machine translation models and how is it distributed across network layers and translation units?
papers.core_contribution: Neural machine translation models learn linguistic representations in a hierarchical manner, with lower layers capturing local morphological information and higher layers capturing global syntactic and semantic dependencies, and the choice of translation unit affects what linguistic properties are captured.
papers.conclusion: Neural machine translation models learn a significant amount of linguistic information in a hierarchical manner without direct supervision, with different layers specializing in different linguistic phenomena.
papers.key_findings:
Word morphology and part-of-speech information are captured at the lower layers of the model.
Lexical semantics and non-local syntactic and semantic dependencies are better represented at the higher layers of the model.
Representations learned using characters are more informed about word morphology compared to those learned using subword units.
Representations learned by multilingual models are richer compared to bilingual models.
The target language impacts the kind of information learned; translating into morphologically-poorer languages leads to better source-side word representations.
papers.abstract:
Despite the recent success of deep neural networks in natural language
processing (NLP), their interpretability remains a challenge. We analyze the
representations learned by neural machine translation models at various levels
of granularity and evaluate their quality through relevant extrinsic
properties. In particular, we seek answers to the following questions: (i) How
accurately is word-structure captured within the learned representations, an
important aspect in translating morphologically-rich languages? (ii) Do the
representations capture long-range dependencies, and effectively handle
syntactically divergent languages? (iii) Do the representations capture lexical
semantics? We conduct a thorough investigation along several parameters: (i)
Which layers in the architecture capture each of these linguistic phenomena;
(ii) How does the choice of translation unit (word, character, or subword unit)
impact the linguistic properties captured by the underlying representations?
(iii) Do the encoder and decoder learn differently and independently? (iv) Do
the representations learned by multilingual NMT models capture the same amount
of linguistic information as their bilingual counterparts? Our data-driven,
quantitative evaluation illuminates important aspects in NMT models and their
ability to capture various linguistic phenomena. We show that deep NMT models
learn a non-trivial amount of linguistic information. Notable findings include:
i) Word morphology and part-of-speech information are captured at the lower
layers of the model; (ii) In contrast, lexical semantics or non-local syntactic
and semantic dependencies are better represented at the higher layers; (iii)
Representations learned using characters are more informed about wordmorphology
compared to those learned using subword units; and (iv) Representations learned
by multilingual models are richer compared to bilingual models.

papers.title: Disentangling Direction and Magnitude in Transformer Representations: A Double Dissociation Through L2-Matched Perturbation Analysis
papers.research_question: What are the distinct functional roles of direction (orientation) and magnitude (norm) in transformer hidden state representations?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces L2-matched perturbation analysis to discover a double dissociation: angular perturbations disproportionately damage language modeling loss, while magnitude perturbations disproportionately damage syntactic accuracy, with distinct mechanistic pathways through attention and LayerNorm.
papers.conclusion: Direction and magnitude serve partially distinct computational roles in LayerNorm-based transformers: direction preferentially governs attentional routing, while magnitude encodes structural position and modulates processing intensity through LayerNorm.
papers.key_findings:
Angular perturbations cause up to 42.9× more damage to language modeling loss than magnitude perturbations at equal Euclidean displacement.
Magnitude perturbations cause up to 20.4% greater drop in syntactic accuracy (subject-verb agreement) than angular perturbations.
Causal intervention shows angular damage is substantially mediated by attention pathways (28.4% recovery via repair), while magnitude damage is substantially mediated by LayerNorm pathways (29.9% recovery).
The dissociation pattern replicates across scales within the Pythia architecture family but reverses in RMSNorm-based architectures like TinyLlama.
Magnitude correlates with parse tree depth, and disrupting this correlation explains why magnitude perturbations specifically impair syntactic processing.
papers.limitation:
L2 matching assumes equal Euclidean distance makes perturbations comparable, but neural networks operate in anisotropic spaces; angular perturbations amplify 3× more than magnitude by the final layer.
Angular perturbations use random orthogonal directions; results might differ for systematic rotations toward known feature directions.
Findings are specific to the Pythia/OPT architecture family and do not generalize to all transformers; the pattern reverses in RMSNorm-based architectures (TinyLlama).
Only middle layers (8–15) were targeted for intervention; early and late layers may show different patterns.
Syntactic evaluation is limited to subject-verb agreement from BLiMP; other syntactic phenomena may show different patterns.
Causal repair experiments account for only ~30% of each perturbation's damage; the remaining ~70% likely flows through MLP layers and residual connections.
future_direction: Feature-specific rotations (systematic rotations toward/away from known feature directions).
Investigating how the roles of direction and magnitude evolve during training.
Exploring magnitude as a confidence signal for uncertainty quantification.
Extending the methodology to other modalities (e.g., vision transformers).
Systematic comparison across normalization schemes (LayerNorm vs. RMSNorm).
papers.abstract: Transformer hidden states encode information as high-dimensional vectors, yet whether direction (orientation in representational space) and magnitude (vector norm) serve distinct functional roles remains unclear. Studying Pythia-family models, we discover a striking cross-over dissociation: angular perturbations cause up to 42.9 more damage to language modeling loss, while magnitude perturbations cause disproportionately more damage to syntactic processing (20.4% vs.1.6% accuracy drop on subject-verb agreement).This finding is enabled by L2-matched perturbation analysis, a methodology ensuring that an gular and magnitude perturbations achieve identical Euclidean displacements. Causal intervention reveals that angular damage flows substantially through the attention pathways (28.4% loss recovery via attention repair), while magnitude damage flows partly through the LayerNorm pathways(29.9% recovery via LayerNorm repair). These patterns replicate across scales within the Pythia architecture family. These findings provide evidence that direction and magnitude support partially distinct computational roles in LayerNorm based architectures. The direction preferentially affects attentional routing, while magnitude modulates processing intensity for fine-grained syntactic judgments. We find different patterns in RMSNorm-based architectures, suggesting that the dissociation depends on architectural choices. Our results refine the linear representation hypothesis and have implications for model editing and interpretability research

papers.title: Discovering Salient Neurons in Deep NLP Models
papers.research_question: Can we identify subsets of neurons that learn specific linguistic properties, and how is linguistic knowledge localized, distributed, and affected by fine-tuning in NLP models?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Linguistic Correlation Analysis (LCA) for extracting salient neurons in NLP models, revealing that linguistic knowledge is localized in lower layers for basic properties and distributed in higher layers for complex concepts, with variations across models and during fine-tuning.
papers.conclusion: The LCA method provides insights into how linguistic knowledge is encoded in neurons, showing localization patterns and redistribution during fine-tuning, with implications for model understanding and transfer learning.
papers.key_findings:
Small subsets of neurons can predict different linguistic tasks.
Neurons for basic lexical information are localized in lower layers, while those for complex concepts are in higher layers.
Linguistic information is redundantly preserved across neurons.
During transfer learning, salient linguistic neurons relocate to lower layers in some models like RoBERTa and XLNet.
Multilingual models exhibit similar neuron distribution for concepts across different languages.
future_direction: Pinpointing specific concepts regressed to lower layers versus those retained in higher layers during fine-tuning.
papers.abstract: While a lot of work has been done in understanding representations learned within deep NLP models and what knowledge they capture, little attention has been paid towards individual neurons. We present a technique called as Linguistic Correlation Analysis to extract salient neurons in the model, with respect to any extrinsic property - with the goal of understanding how such a knowledge is preserved within neurons. We carry out a fine-grained analysis to answer the following questions: (i) can we identify subsets of neurons in the network that capture specific linguistic properties? (ii) how localized or distributed neurons are across the network? iii) how redundantly is the information preserved? iv) how fine-tuning pre-trained models towards downstream NLP tasks, impacts the learned linguistic knowledge? iv) how do architectures vary in learning different linguistic properties? Our data-driven, quantitative analysis illuminates interesting findings: (i) we found small subsets of neurons that can predict different linguistic tasks, ii) with neurons capturing basic lexical information (such as suffixation) localized in lower most layers, iii) while those learning complex concepts (such as syntactic role) predominantly in middle and higher layers, iii) that salient linguistic neurons are relocated from higher to lower layers during transfer learning, as the network preserve the higher layers for task specific information, iv) we found interesting differences across pre-trained models, with respect to how linguistic information is preserved within, and v) we found that concept exhibit similar neuron distribution across different languages in the multilingual transformer models. Our code is publicly available as part of the NeuroX toolkit.

papers.title: Language Arithmetics: Towards Systematic Language Neuron Identification and Manipulation
papers.research_question: How do language-specific neurons in multilingual LLMs control language behavior, and can they be manipulated to steer model outputs across languages?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces language arithmetics, an additive neuron intervention method, to identify and manipulate language-specific neurons in multilingual LLMs, showing that it can steer language generation and improve performance on downstream tasks.
papers.conclusion: Our large-scale study demonstrates that language-specific neurons encode meaningful linguistic features that can be identified, analyzed, and manipulated to steer model behavior across languages. By employing a novel additive intervention method, we show that activating these neurons allows for generation language control and improves performance on various multilingual tasks.
papers.key_findings:
Language-specific neurons cluster in deeper layers, with non-Latin scripts showing greater specialization.
Related languages share overlapping neurons, reflecting linguistic proximity.
Additive language arithmetics outperforms replacement-based methods for language forcing.
Activating target-language neurons improves performance on multilingual tasks like translation, QA, comprehension, and NLI.
Models exhibit internal 'fallback' mechanisms for language selection when dominant language neurons are deactivated.
papers.limitation:
Broader evaluation across more diverse downstream settings is needed.
Quality and fluency of forced outputs across languages, especially low-resource ones, remain underexplored.
Analysis focuses on isolated neurons, overlooking distributed representations and circuits.
Computational constraints limited some experiments to smaller models.
future_direction: Investigate the interactions and dependencies between neurons to understand network-level mechanisms supporting multilingual processing.
More detailed investigation of language fallback dynamics.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) exhibit strong multilingual abilities, yet the neural mechanisms behind language-specific processing remain unclear. We analyze language-specific neurons in Llama-3.1-8B, Mistral-Nemo-12B, and Aya-Expanse-8B & 32B across 21 typologically diverse languages, identifying neurons that control language behavior. Using the Language Activation Probability Entropy (LAPE) method, we show that these neurons cluster in deeper layers, with non-Latin scripts showing greater specialization. Related languages share overlapping neurons, reflecting internal representations of linguistic proximity. Through language arithmetics, i.e. systematic activation addition and multiplication, we steer models to deactivate unwanted languages and activate desired ones, outperforming simpler replacement approaches. These interventions effectively guide behavior across five multilingual tasks: language forcing, translation, QA, comprehension, and NLI. Manipulation is more successful for high-resource languages, while typological similarity improves effectiveness. We also demonstrate that cross-lingual neuron steering enhances downstream performance and reveal internal "fallback" mechanisms for language selection when neurons are progressively deactivated. Our code is made publicly available at https://github.com/d-gurgurov/Language-Neurons-Manipulation.

papers.title: Behind the Scene: Revealing the Secrets of Pre-trained Vision-and-Language Models
papers.research_question: How do pre-trained vision-and-language models work internally? Specifically, the paper investigates multimodal fusion, modality importance, cross-modal interaction, visual relations, and linguistic knowledge in these models.
